subtopic: MESSAGE OP PRIMP, MINISTER CHURCHILL AND PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT TO THE PEOPLE OP ITALY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MESSAGE OP PRIMP, MINISTER CHURCHILL AND PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT TO THE PEOPLE OP ITALY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning Prime Minister Churchill and President Roosevelt issued a proclamation addressed to the people of Italy, setting forth that the sole hope for Italy's survival lies in honourable capitulation. The following is the text of the proclamation:
1.	At this moment the combined armed forces of the United States, Great Britain and Canada, under the command of General Eisenhower and his deputy, General Alexander, are carrying the war deep into the territory of your country. This is the direct consequence of the shameful leadership to which you have been subjected by Mussolini and his fascist regime.
2.	Mussolini carried you into this war as the satellite of a brutal destroyer of peoples and liberties.
3.	Mussolini plunged you into a w'ar which he thought Hitler had already won. In spite of Italy's great vulnerability to attack by air and sea, your fascist leaders sent your sons, your ships, your air forces, to distant battlefields to aid Germany in her attempt to conquer England, Russia and the world.
4.	This association with the designs of nazi-controlled Germany was unworthy of Italy's ancient traditions of freedom and culture- traditions to which the peoples of America and Great Britain owe so much.
5.	Your soldiers have fought not in the interests of Italy but for nazi Germany. They have
The War

fought courageously, but they have been betrayed and abandoned by the Germans on the Russian front and on every battlefield in Africa from El Alemein to Cape Bon.
6.	To-day Germany's hope for world conquest have been blasted on all fronts. The skies over Italy are dominated by the vast air armadas of the United States and Great Britain. Italy's sea coasts are threatened by the greatest accumulation of British and allied sea power ever concentrated in the Mediterranean.
7.	The forces now opposed to you are pledged to destroy the power of nazi Germany-power which has ruthlessly been used to inflict slavery, destruction and death on all those who refuse to recognize the Germans as the master race.
8.	The sole hope for Italy's survival lies in honourable capitulation to the overwhelming power of the military forces of the united nations.
9.	If you continue to tolerate the fascist regime which serves the evil power of the nazis, you must suffer the consequences of your own choice. We take no satisfaction in invading Italian soil and bringing the tragic devastation of war home to the Italian people. But we are determined to destroy the false leaders and their doctrines which have brought Italy to her present position.
10.	Every moment that you resist the combined forces of the united nations-every drop of blood that you sacrifice-can serve only one purpose; to give the fascist and nazi leaders a little more time to escape from the inevitable consequences of their own crime.
11.	All your interests and all your traditions have been betrayed by nazi Germany and your own false and corrupt leaders; it is only by destroying both that a reconstituted Italy can hope to occupy a respected place in the family of European nations.
12.	The time has now come for you, Italian people, to consult your own self-respect and your own interests and your own desires for a restoration of national dignity, security and peace. The time has come for you to decide whether Italians shall die for Mussolini and Hitler or live for Italy and for civilization.

subtopic: DISSEMINATION OF NEWS OF LANDING IN SICILY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. BROOKE CLAXTON (Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council) :
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DISSEMINATION OF NEWS OF LANDING IN SICILY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the leader of
the opposition asked, first, for a clarification of a statement I made on Tuesday and, second, in what way the wartime information board played a part in the news of the landing in Sicily. His question referred to newspaper editorials, presumably those in the Ottawa Journal, the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail, which said or implied that credit had been claimed for the wartime information board for the fine stories of Ross Munro. Such a claim would have been preposterous, and such an interpretation was not justified by the record. The actual words referred to by the leader of the opposition were:
The events of the last few days indicate how useful has been the cooperation of the press relations officers, the press associations, the correspondents of newspapers overseas, with the wartime information board at various points in the background, in seeing that the people of this continent got early news of the landing in Sicily, and also that the statements which were made have afterwards received early and favourable notice in the United States both in the press and over the radio.
What the statement did' was to name specifically the other agencies which had to do with this early and favourable notice, and then to add that the wartime information board had done useful work in the background. The limited nature of this assertion was emphasized in two further references, and the general relationship of the board to the press was made plain in numerous references in the speeches of the Prime Minister and myself.
The statement quoted speaks of the "early news of the landing in Sicily". This referred
Wartime Information Board

particularly to the first news of Canadian participation, given in the United States war department communique, and to the Prime Minister's statement, both of which were issued in the first hour of Saturday morning. The dispatches from correspondents with the troops only came more than twenty-four hours later. The facts that word of the Canadians taking part came with the first announcement of the invasion, and that the Prime Minister's statement was issued immediately afterwards, were of prime importance.
The role that the wartime information board had in these early announcements can now be better understood in the light of the Prime Minister's statement yesterday.
The board was in continuous consultation with other officers of the government in endeavouring to see that the first announcement of an invasion included mention of Canadians. It also made arrangements to ensure that the Prime Minister's statement immediately afterwards was quickly and effectively distributed, particularly in the United States. Hon, members will appreciate the importance of the quick distribution of the first statement of Canadian participation from a Canadian source. Had the news about Canadian participation. been delayed for a day, the facts would never fully have caught up with the first impression of the world that only British and American troops were involved and Canadian stories would not have been as well received.
In the statement nothing whatever was said to detract from the work in Sicily of Mr. Ross Munro or other correspondents, or of the Canadian Press itself. Mr. Munro's despatches were superb. They have done much to tell the Canadian people vividly about their troops in action, for which I did not for a moment claim credit for the wartime information board. In this case the board had to do with the early announcements and the quick and effective distribution of the first statement about Canadian participation emanating from Canada.
The extreme importance of the work of the war correspondents stands out and is fully recognized. In the field the three services maintain public relations officers who were formerly trained newspapermen themselves. The British and American armies also maintain public relations services. Their full-time duty is to assist war correspondents in obtaining and transmitting material and- facilitating their work in every conceivable way. The public relations officers of the armed forces, under Mr. J. W. G. Clark, work in very close

cooperation with the wartime information board. Working together they supplied background material on the Canadian army to supplement news from the front and gain credit for the people to whom it should be given, namely, the Canadian soldiers who are at this moment in battle with the enemy.

subtopic: DISSEMINATION OF NEWS OF LANDING IN SICILY
speechtext: It is still not very clear to me how the wartime information board had anything to do with respect to the news which reached the Prime Minister and was then disseminated, because it would come through the ordinary press channels. The Prime Minister then gave his statement to the public. Therefore it is not clear to me how the board can still claim to have taken any significant part with respect to what happened last Friday night or last Saturday.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DISSEMINATION OF NEWS OF LANDING IN SICILY
speechtext: My hon. friend must appreciate that the full story cannot be told or the usefulness of a good deal of the board's work might disappear. I could tell my hon. friend this, that even on Thursday officers of the board were in almost continuous consultation.with officers of other departments considering the situation and working towards the end that the Prime Minister achieved. On Friday the office in Washington was kept continually manned with ticker services from various directions, and possibly the first word to reach Ottawa of the American communiques from Algiers and the Pentagon building were sent in- from Washington. Then the statement of the Prime Minister was sent back to Washington and was given very early and favourable attention in the American press.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to confirm the transfer of certain lands to Ontario and Quebec effected by order in council of the 26th day of January, 1943.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am not sure whether the minister has given any explanation of the object of this resolution, or any statement of the principle of the bill to be founded upon it. I think this is the appropriate time for a short statement from the minister.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Chairman, I think before making a statement I should table a bill of the legislature of Ontario assented to on February 19, 1943, and a bill of the legislature of Quebec assented to on May 20, 1943, both dealing with the ratification of an agreement made between these two provinces and dated January 2, 1943.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Will the minister also table the order in council referred to in the resolution?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The order in council has already been tabled, and copies of it are printed as annexes to the bills of the two provincial legislatures. For the convenience of members of the committee who may be interested I have secured additional copies of these bills and I will now make them available to hon. members, a certain number of them having been made available to me by the clerk of the Ontario legislature and likewise by the clerk of the Quebec legislature.
To state very shortly what is involved, the resolution refers to whter powers on the Ottawa river. The Ottawa river, as all hon. members know, is interprovincial. There have been developments on that river but there are still available water powers susceptible of developing as much as 900,000 horse-power. Those powers could not be developed without an agreement between the provinces. The Ottawa river is regarded as a navigable river, and the extent of the private rights in the Ottawa river depends, of course, on the respective laws of Ontario on the one side and of Quebec on the other. The Ontario government was desirous of
developing additional water powers on the upper reaches of the Ottawa river, and the governments of the two provinces came to the conclusion that it would be more practical if they made an exchange of their respective rights so that one province would have the whole of the water powers at one point and the other province the whole of the water powers at the other point. They could then set about developing their respective properties in the manner which would suit the requirements and convenience of the people of their respective provinces.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There are five power sites involved?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are five power sites involved, and the arrangement they arrived at was that Carillon, which is the one lowest down, Rocher-Fendu, which is the third, and one-half of Paquette, would go to the province of Quebec, and that Chenaux, which is between Carillon and Rocher-Fendu, would go to Ontario, and that the two upper sites, Des Joachims and Cave and Foumeaux, also go to Ontario.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The effect of that would be to alter somewhat the interprovincial boundaries?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, not to alter the interprovincial boundaries but to alter the
property rights vested in the crown in the right of each respective province. The arange-ments do not provide for permanent grants; they are very long-term leases.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
That, I think, raises one of the principal points in connection with the proposed legislation. There are those who believe that this is a device, though I do not use the word in an offensive way, by which the boundaries of two provinces are being changed, not by an exchange of deed of land, but nevertheless on an extremely long-term lease which actually has the same effect in the end as an exchange of properties, and by virtue of that it is an alteration in the actual boundary lines between the provinces. The point involved, which the minister will see very quickly, is that to set such a precedent goes to the root of the British North America Act; for I think it is generally understood that provinces by agreement cannot alter the boundary lines set by the British North America Act, which is a statute of the parliament of the United Kingdom. Whether. or not the government has succeeded by virtue of a device with respect to a long-term lease in avoiding the constitutional point which would be raised were deeds to be given and the boundary line thereby changed, constitutes

Transfer of Lands
one of the main constitutional legal points which this legislation raises. I should like the Minister of Justice to give his views about it, because it is in the minds of many people at the moment.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think the discussion of the point requires any very long debate. The bill before this house would not have been necessary at all had there not been some proprietary rights of the dominion in connection with one or other or several of these sites. The agreement between the provinces purports to vest on the one hand in the Quebec streams commission and on the other hand in the Ontario hydro certain leasehold rights. The Ontario hydro can come into Quebec and acquire leasehold rights without affecting in any way the territorial boundaries of Quebec, and the Quebec streams commission can likewise acquire in Ontario leasehold rights without that having any effect upon the boundaries of the two provinces.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
They are both corporations.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They are both corporations acting and holding for the crown in the respective areas of the two provinces. But that would no more alter the boundaries of the provinces than if the Ontario hydro were acquiring a farm to raise produce to feed the employees attending one of its undertakings. The arrangement between these two provinces would have been made without any reference to the federal government at all had it not been that the government of the united Canadas prior to confederation had made some improvements to assist in navigation and in the floating of logs, and by virtue of the distribution of proprietary rights at confederation retained such improvements as had been made for that purpose. Hon. members will recall that a few years ago there was a reference to the supreme court to determine which government would own water powers which might be improved or increased or made available by the existence of these federal improvements, and the court, following opinions which had been expressed by the privy council, was very guarded in its language and it is not easy to find any definite pronouncement in that regard in the judgment which was rendered.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Was that a
reference?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That was a reference to the supreme court.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Therefore it was rather ineffective.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: There was no concrete case involved. The court, in a learned discussion of the old law, refrained from making a pronouncement which would have any concrete effect on any specific water-power.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
My recollection is that the effect of the judgment was practically nil.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think it might be put in this way: the dominion asserted, through counsel representing it before the supreme court, that it had proprietary rights in water powers, and the court refused to accept the view put forward by the dominion government.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
One other question. As I appreciate the situation on these interprovincial streams, the minister stated that the river is declared to be a navigable river; therefore we have a substantial interest under that question of navigation. What is the position with respect to that in this matter? Is there any interference or anything of the kind?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. The agreements all provide that all these plans will have to be submitted for examination and approval under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Nothing can be done without the detailed plans being submitted and the usual undertakings being made. The plans will not be approved, of course, if they provide for any interference contrary to public interest with navigation at the time they are submitted. There is also an undertaking on the part of those who submit plans for approval that if in the future conditions should arise where public interest would require modifications to be made, the owner of the works will have to make them.
This legislation does not envisage the Quebec streams commission on the one hand and the Ontario hydro on the other as anything more than companies, corporations, and the reason for the legislation is that the Dominion has certain proprietary rights, not the same on the two sides. Under Quebec laws, as hon. members know, along navigable waters the riparian rights stop at the high water mark, whilst I understand that under the common law it is at least contended that even in navigable streams they may extend out to midstream.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes. It depends somewhat on the original grants.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The federal government did own some portion of the shores along these various stretches of river which would be affected by the development of the water powers.

Transfer of Lands

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
That is at Carillon.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: At Carillon and also above Des Joachims; and the developments could not prudently be made without acquiring these shore rights.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
In other words, the federal government has a proprietary interest in part of these power sites.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Possibly in a small part of the Carillon power site; probably not in any other of the power sites, though it may have shore property.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Flowage rights.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. The companies or corporation, or commissions, whatever they may be, to make the development would have to acquire these rights from individuals by mutual arrangement or by expropriation proceedings. They could not expropriate against the dominion government' the federal crown, and the arrangement that was made was that the federal government would cede to them such riparian rights, flowage rights, or whatever it may be, as would be necessary for the execution of development work. The view was taken that the people of Canada whether inhabitants of one province or another, were Canadians and that if this was something that constituted a valuable natural resource it was in the interests of the Canadian people that it be developed and used when there was need for the power that could be produced, and that it would not be proper for the dominion government to take an attitude that would prevent the use of these water powers in the interests of the public generally when the proper time arrived for development.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
In other
words, we could not adopt a dog-in-the-manger attitude-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
-and say, "You cannot appropriate against us"; that would retard development. When the minister uses the word "cede" does he mean give, or are they to pay?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	No; they are
transferred. They are not properties of considerable value outside of their, shall I say nuisance value in connection with the development of water power.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Have they no strategic value?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	No strategic value
for purposes of defence.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I mean, for the purpose of water power. I do not know the situation; I am just asking.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member, as a lawyer advising a corporation, would say, "Well now, don't attempt to go ahead until you get that; it is something without which you would not have the kind of title I would recommend for a bond issue."

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext: It might be valuable.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
lit is
valuable.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: How that kind of value can be measured it is very difficult to determine, as was shown in the famous Cedar Rapids case, which was for years before the courts and went twice to the privy council.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The value is the value to the owner, not to the taker.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The value to the
owner is something very difficult to measure, but under these conditions we thought it would not be proper for the dominion government to be very particular about that. At the time this was done the provision of additional power was looked upon as of considerable interest to the war effort of the country; the Ontario hydro was prepared to make an investment which it was estimated might run into $40,000,000 to provide power, and perhaps the few hundreds or thousands of dollars that might have been established as value to the owner of these rights was not looked upon as a consideration that should stand in the way at all; after all the federal and provincial purses were all purses of the people of Canada, so that it was not very important to have any exact figure assessed. What was arranged was that in order to facilitate this exchange between the two provinces, and to allow each to have control of a certain portion of the sites, the federal government should abandon such rights as it might have.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The question of joint development was not considered, or not agreed upon?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	It was found that
because of the difference in the situation between the two provinces the interests were not similar. Quebec at the present time does not consider that it is in its interests to develop any more water powers.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
After
Arvida or Shipshaw you have quite a surplus.
Transfer of Lands

Mr. ST. LAURENT:	After the war we
shall have quite a surplus there, and there is always development on the St. Lawrence. That is looked upon as a possibility, and if that were done it would provide such an enormous block of power that it would not be of practical advantage to have these other sites developed now.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
And there is the location of the power.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Ontario did feel that it would suit the conveniences of its public and of its commission to develop these upper sites of the Ottawa immediately.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext: May I ask a question in reference to the development of the Ottawa river? The federal government apparently has nothing to do with the development of electricity, but it has to do with everything pertaining to navigation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONFIRM TRANSFER TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC EFFECTED BY ORDER IN COUNCIL

subtopic: ACTIONS BY OR AGAINST THE CROWN-STATUS OF MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Exchequer Court Act to provide that for the purpose of determining liability in any action or other proceeding by or against His Majesty, a person who was at any time since the tw'enty-fourth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight, a member of the naval, military or air forces of His Majesty in right of Canada shall be deemed to have been at such time a servant of the crown.

subtopic: ACTIONS BY OR AGAINST THE CROWN-STATUS OF MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Will the minister state what the scope of the bill will be?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The scope of the bill will be only as set out in the resolution.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

subtopic: ACTIONS BY OR AGAINST THE CROWN-STATUS OF MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
This resolution arises out of a decision of the exchequer court in the King v. McArthur which reaffirmed the principle that a member of the naval, military or air forces of his majesty, being an enlisted man, was not a servant of the crown in the sense of the Exchequer Court Act. I think this legislation is a measure of justice, but it does not go quite far enough. I have no quarrel on legal grounds with the decision in the King v. McArthur, because I think it is based on the English decisions, and I believe also there have been one or two Canadian decisions. My point is that the right to sue the crown is still being limited to actions in the exchequer court.
I suggest that the day has arrived in Canada at least, if not elsewhere, when consideration -I shall limit it to that-should be given to providing for the subject the right to sue the crown in any provincial court. I recall the reasons why this has been limited heretofore to the exchequer court. One of them is that it prevents fictitious or small claims being

Exchequer Court Act
raised against the crown through the necessity of having to go to the exchequer court and having to obtain a fiat before the crown can be sued. We are living in a changing world. To-day the crown is engaged in big business. To-day the crown is spending in its activities, including of course the armed forces, over half the national income. Never in the history of the nation has the crown been so much engaged in business as it is to-day, and not in the business of government alone. The crown is engaged in commercial business through various channels and organizations and agencies and commissions. I think the time has come when the right should be granted to the subject of his majesty, resident in Canada, to sue the crown in any court of competent jurisdiction based upon the domicile or residence of the claimant. Vice versa, the crown should have the right if it so wishes to sue the subject in any of these courts. I put this on the ground of changing operations of our national economy. There was a time when you could not sue the crown at all, and there are certain provinces which still deny to the subject the right to sue the crown. I think in my own province, unless the law has been altered within recent months, there is no opportunity of suing the government of New Brunswick on any ground, contractual or in tort, and that is very often a denial of justice. What does a man have to do? He has to go with his hat in his hand to the government of the day in the province of New Brunswick and get redress ex gratia, not as a matter of right. That is an intolerable situation. As my hon. friend the member for Rosedale remarks, it is a relic of the feudal system. We have in Canada a better system. We have a petition of right. But even there a man is not always certain that he will be able to get his case before an independent court. He has to run the gauntlet, we will say, of the Minister of Justice. I am bound to say that I have never known of a case, and I have had a good many cases in days gone by considering the limited practice I had, where, if one were able to make out a prima facie case, a fiat was refused. But there has been such delay, at times, and expense. You have to employ an agent in Ottawa and brief him with the facts if there is any dispute about the matter, and it is a costly system, a cumbersome system.
I am making a plea here and now for a change in the system so as to put the crown which now is developing into such a big business manager in the same category as the subject. The days of the feudal system are over; the days when the crown can be said
to do no wrong are long since past. The crown is often through its servants guilty of malfeasance and of non-feasance, and why should it not be subject to the jurisdiction of the provincial courts? Surely it cannot be that the crown would not get justice in the provincial courts, especially in this day when trial by jury of civil actions in the provincial courts has been very largely abolished by statute. I hold quite strong views on this subject, and I am stating them now in the hope that those charged with authority will give some consideration to them. I should like to have an expression of opinion from the membership of this house, especially those who belong to the legal profession.
I have in mind the case of a widow whose husband was killed through the allegedly gross negligence of an army truck driver. I have been endeavouring to obtain through certain departments of the government an explanation of the facts, what the inquiry disclosed, in order to permit the widow to get redress. I am not going into the details of the case, but if that woman has a cause of action, what redress will she have? I do not think she can ever bring action in the exchequer court. She has to depend on the good will, shall we say, of the authorities here in Ottawa if she can show that she has suffered the loss of her support by reason of the negligence of a servant of the crown. If this bill passes she has to go to the Exchequer Court of Canada to assert her rights. I suggest to the membership of this house that in this enlightened day and generation that is not good enough. She should be allowed to sue in the courts of her own province and have the case tried at the most convenient point in the county in which she lives. Anybody who has had anything to do with trials in the exchequer court knows that in the provinces the court sits once a year-oftener, I assume, if there is any quantity of litigation, but as a rule in New Brunswick it sits once a year, and if you start your action after the last session of court you have to wait a year for it to be tried. I could go on and argue this at great length and support the argument with cogent reasons, but I do not propose to delay the committee further. I hope that consideration will be given to the matter now, because it is important. It is a matter of justice to the subjects of His Majesty in Canada who may have a cause of action against the crown.
I think this bill is a matter of justice- that is, justice in the abstract. I am going to support the bill. The matter is already covered I think by order in council, but this
Exchequer Court Act

will make it part of the permanent substantive law of the country and it can be repealed only by act of parliament. I am sorry there are not more members of the legal profession here to-day, because I should like to hear their views. As for me, I have no manner of doubt at all, having regard to the multiplicity of activities in which the crown is engaged to-day outside of war altogether but due to the war, that the crown should be made liable for actions in tort for negligence on the part of its servants and in actions ex contractu and be answerable in a court of competent jurisdiction in the province in which the complainant resides.

subtopic: ACTIONS BY OR AGAINST THE CROWN-STATUS OF MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I think the Minister of
Justice is to be commended for introducing this bill to amend the Exchequer Court Act. When it becomes law, claims against the crown for death or injury to the person or for damages to property caused by the negligence of a member of the armed forces can be adjudicated by our courts.
There are one or two other amendments which in my opinion should be made to the Exchequer Court Act. One is the amendment which has been suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury. The crown can go into any of the provinces of the dominion and start an action against a citizen in any of our courts, and there is no reason why the citizens of any province should not be in a similar position. It seems to me that a citizen of any of our provinces should have the right to commence an action against the crown in any court of the province having jurisdiction in civil actions.
There is one other amendment to the act which I think should be made. The exchequer court was created by an act which came into force on October 30, 1887. Section 19 of that act provides that the court shall have exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine certain matters therein set out. Then follow a number of clauses setting forth the nature of the claims that can be adjudicated.
To quote from the judgment of Mr. Justice Newcombe in the case of the Canadian National Railways v. St. John Motor Line Limited (1930), 72, S.C.R., p.488:
These clauses must be read in the light of the decisions, of which the earlier leading examples are mentioned in the case of Ryder versus The King; and by these and the later authorities it is well established in this court that not only does the Exchequer Court acquire jurisdiction to adjudicate the classes of claims above described, but also that in such cases liability

is imposed upon the crown to respond in damages for the negligence of its officers or servants where, in the like circumstances, such a liability would rest upon a subject corporation or individual-
Here are the important words:

according to the law of the province in which the claim arose, as that law existed at the time when the Exchequer Court Act began to operate.
The exchequer court began to operate in 1887. Or, to put the matter in other words, when an action is brought for any of the claims enumerated under section 19, "liability was to be determined by the general laws of the several provinces in force at the time such liability was imposed," to quote the words of Mr. Justice, afterwards Chief Justice, Davies, in Armstrong v. the King (1908) 40 Can.

The law of negligence in some of the provinces has been changed in more than one important particular since the year 1887, when the exchequer court came into being. In 1887 in all the provinces in which the common law prevailed a person could not succeed in an action for damages based on negligence if it was proved that he had in any degree contributed to the accident, or perhaps it would be better to say, if he was guilty of contributory negligence. To-day this principle has ceased to be law in several of the provinces. The admiralty rule that in such cases the damages were in proportion to the degree that the parties to the action were at fault has replaced the common law rule.
Again., in 1887 a person was entitled to damages if while being driven as a guest or invitee he suffered injuries through the negligence of his host. In. many of the provinces to-day, under our motor vehicles acts, we have what is known as the guest rule, which provides that a person who has accepted an invitation to be driven in an automobile cannot obtain damages for the injuries he sustains through the negligence of the owner of the vehicle or his servant. Neither of these laws is recognized by the Exchequer Court of Canada because they were not in force in 1887.
A resident of one of the provinces where these statutes are in force-let us say New Brunswick-brings an action in the exchequer court against the crown under section 19 of the act. The plaintiff claims he is entitled to damages because the law of the province in which he lives provides that under the state of facts that he can prove he is entitled to damages. The court says no, that does not necessarily follow; it is not what the law is in your province to-day that matters, but what matters is what the law in your province was in 1887.

Exchequer Court Act
The law of the province should govern in such cases. It is unsatisfactory for a citizen in any province to learn that the law of his province does not necessarily apply to actions which are brought by him in the exchequer court.
I feel very strongly that the Exchequer Court Act should be amended to provide that the provincial acts, such as the Contributory Negligence Act and the provisions of the motor vehicles acts respecting guests who are driven in cars, should be binding on the exchequer court, and I would ask the minister if he will not give that matter some consideration, discuss it with the officials of his department, and perhaps with the judges of the exchequer court as well.
It is an extraordinary situation, it seems to me, as I have said, that after a person brings an action for negligence in the exchequer court and states that under a certain set of facts he is entitled in his province to damages, the exchequer court says no, you are not entitled to damages because in 1887 the law of your province was not as it is to-day, or, because the law of your province was different. I submit that that is a wholly unsatisfactory state of affairs.
Anomalous.

Yes, it is an anomalous state of affairs.
I was going to speak about the matter which the hon. member for York-Sunbury brought up, that the subject should have the right to sue the crown not only in the exchequer court but in any other court of Canada. I think that steps should be taken to have an amendment or amendments made to enable that to be done.

I wish briefly to support the hon. member for York-Sunbury in his representation to the minister that consideration be given to having the Exchequer Court Act amended or power given to our various provincial courts, according to their jurisdiction, to try actions against the crown. I agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury that the time is coming when we shall have to give these conveniences to the Canadian public. We are developing to the extent that we should leave behind this idea of having to come to Ottawa, go through a long procedure, issue a petition of right, and get the consent of the Minister of Justice to start an action. We should be more realistic.
I am glad also that this particular resolution has been brought in by the Minister of Justice. I think it is due and proper.

I should like to endorse the stand taken by the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon. member for St. John-Albert. I hope the Minister of Justice will explain fully to the committee why it is that provision has not been made along the lines they suggest. If our courts are to serve the public it is high time that these changes were made; and certainly it is very inconvenient that people living in the distant provinces can sue only in the exchequer court. It hits us particularly hard. I do suggest that provision be made for suing in our provincial courts.

I should like to urge upon the minister that the two matters referred to, first, by myself and more particularly the point raised by the hon. member for St. John-Albert are reforms that are long overdue. I am glad the hon. member for St. John-Albert brought up that point. It escaped my attention. I am pleased that he has made such a lucid exposition of the point. It is an anomalous situation that while jurisdiction is given under a statute to entertain an action, the statute creating the jurisdiction is so rigid that it fastens the claimant to the legal position as at the date of the passing of the legislation. It has neither flexibility nor regard to the changing conditions and the changing state of the law. I think the hon. member for St. John-Albert is to be congratulated upon raising that point, and in my opinion it is really of more primary fundamental importance than the point I raised myself. But the two points together should be considered by the minister and he should give effect to them.
They are both very important.
Yes.

I cannot speak as a lawyer on this question, and I am not versed in the legal technicalities involved, but as a layman I have received, since coming to Ottawa, considerable correspondence regarding cases such as those referred to by the hon. member for York-Sunbury and others, and I have reason to know that there is a great deal of discontent in the public mind at the present time regarding the inability of the subject to get justice where the crown is involved. The hon. member for York-Sunbury called attention to the case of the King v. McArthur. I have a considerable amount of correspondence on that case from people who knew that man, who knew the circumstances and followed the case through the lengthy trial and read the lengthy report given upon it.
Exchequer Court Act

But the crown did raise this as a defence in that ease.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The crown used to raise as a subsidiary defence that members of the forces were not servants of the crown within the meaning of the act. The learned judge in the McArthur case decided on both grounds, that there was not sufficient evidence of negligence and that in any event a member of the armed forces was not a servant of the crown within the meaning of the act. Had there been only that reason given it would have been proper to say, "If you are going to amend the act we will give the man in connection with whose case the matter arises the benefit of the amendment." But to determine or have determined by parliament, without consideration of the evidence, that that judgment was wrong on the facts would be something I would not care to recommend to the house.
About the other matters, I do thank hon. members for expressing their views upon the point. I will not make any long statement but will merely explain that the reason for the decision, that it is the law of 1887 that has still to be applied by the exchequer court, is of course the logical conclusion from the rule that the crown is not bound by legislation unless expressly mentioned. The crown accepted liability in 1887 for a certain situation as it then existed. No amendments made since can bind the crown unless the crown 
is specially mentioned and unless it is passed by competent authority. The provinces could not, even if they wanted to, extend their legislation in such a way as to increase the liability of the crown in the right of the dominion government, and the suggestion that is made is that we cancel that additional rule with respect to liability arising out of negligence. The old rule that the crown is not bound unless expressly mentioned is being applied-

It could be done another way.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Well, it could be done from time to time; we could say: We will accept the situation as it is to-day.

Or as it may be in various jurisdictions.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Well, that would be a contradiction of the rule and future legislation would affect the crown without its being specially mentioned. With respect to these prerogatives, they are sometimes referred to as having come down to us from feudal times, but there are still prerogatives in the crown that cannot be lightly wiped out of the general system of our laws. This matter will be given serious consideration. It would be of course a matter of government policy because it involves increasing the liability, but consideration will be given to the question whether or not it will be proper to accept the legislation as it exists at the present time. We know what that is. We know how far it goes.

At least that would bring us up to date.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That would bring us up to date; and I do confess that since 1887 there has been a substantial change in conditions to which it is worth giving careful consideration. On the other point, as to whether or not jurisdiction to extend the claimant's case against the crown should be given to all provincial courts, that will be given further consideration, though I must say that it has been given careful consideration by several departments of government, and the reason the bill as it is was drawn in that way was that it was felt it would not be proper to have a system whereby in one section of the country an individual could recover from the crown, while, if he happens to live in another section of the country he would not recover from the same crown under exactly the same circumstances.

What is that? I did not hear that.

Exchequer Court Act
Mr. ST. LAURENT: "VVe want uniformity of liability on the part of the dominion government. The dominion government raises its funds from the whole Canadian people. We think it only proper that the liability of the crown to the subject should be the same no matter where the subject lives, and we feel that if we did not have the exchequer court to apply uniform rules to claims against the crown we might have claims being maintained in one portion of the country on facts with respect to which claims would not be maintained in another part.

In other words you say there would be different rules of law in different jurisdictions?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	There would be
different rules of law and different degrees of latitude or elasticity in the application of the rules, and that was thought undesirable when dealing with the federal crown. Whether or not that be a good and sufficient reason, that is why no provision was made at this time for extending jurisdiction to the provincial courts. In that connection I may say that *the officers of the department will confer or are conferring-I think the matter is already under way-with the exchequer court officers to bring about a scale of costs that will not be out of proportion to what costs would be incurred in provincial jurisdictions. Moreover, a rule has been established that in motor accidents or things of that kind, where there is apt to be a counterclaim, we would not proceed in provincial courts, and thus put the defendant in the position where he could not assert a counterclaim. If we should proceed in a provincial court against a defendant because of a collision, and he should contend that the collision was the fault of our servant and that he should be the one to recover, he cannot urge his claim against us in a provincial court.

Under the
present system. '
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Under the present system. There were some cases in which that point had arisen, and we decided to withdraw those cases from the provincial courts and institute them in the exchequer court because we consider it only fair that if we are claiming we should make our claim in such form that if the defendant has a counterclaim to assert, he may submit it at the same time and have them both passed upon in one decision.

Otherwise he would be very seriously prejudiced.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He would be prejudiced; he would have to meet our claim in
the provincial court and then submit a new claim in the exchequer court and go all over the whole thing again.

That principle is sound.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is something we are going to avoid. We will not now, in connection with these claims, go to the provincial courts; not because we do not think we would get justice there, but because if we do go there we put the defendant at a disadvantage and in some instances prevent him from asserting his counterclaim.

Of course that could be taken care of by legislation here.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It could be taken care of by legislation, but still it would involve restricting the prerogatives of the crown. Before I came to the department I had views on that matter, but I have not been in the department long enough to feel entitled to be too drastic in wiping out prerogatives which have come down through the centuries and which have justification to a certain extent. I confess that circumstances are not what they were in 1887. That is something to which we shall have to give serious consideration, but how far we can go is a matter to which we must give not only serious but careful consideration; for what we do is done for all time. You can never increase a royal prerogative, or at least I do not foresee that for many generations there will be any opportunity to add to these prerogatives of the crown. So that whenever you take something away it is definitely gone, and that makes it necessary to proceed with care.

I am in agreement with the last observation made by the minister. I am no iconoclast, yet I am not very much impressed by this question of the prerogatives of the crown. The crown still has a great many prerogatives. If you listen to what goes on in this house in connection with the expenditure of money you will realize that theoretically not a dollar can be spent unless the king's representative first recommends it, and that is a pretty strong position to take.
I think good may come out of this discussion. If time permits I hope the minister will discuss the matter with the officials of his department and if the opportunity offers I hope he will take it up in council. I am not very hopeful, for " out of sight, out of mind." I am of the opinion that one reason why jurisdiction has never been conferred upon the
National Revenue Act

provincial courts in connection with any of these actions is that there is a feeling in government that the present restrictive jurisdiction to bring actions against the crown does away with vexatious and frivolous actions. That may be true, and perhaps otherwise the crown would be sued very much more frequently than it is to-day; yet the case I have attempted to describe shows the hardship that may be imposed upon the subject. Here is a woman who is claiming under Lord Campbell's act, with her husband killed1 through the alleged negligence of what is now a servant of the crown, and she has to go to the exchequer court to get redress. I think in this twentieth century we ought to facilitate the position of people in that category.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury made a strong plea in favour of dispensing with the petition of right in the exchequer court. Is there any reason why that practice should be continued in the present day? Would not thirty days' or sixty days' notice that the man intended to sue be sufficient, without having to go to the expense of a petition of right?

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 78, respecting the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it may be of assistance to the committee if I make a few brief comments on the bill now under consideration.
There are at present over 1,600 Indian reserves in the province of British Columbia. To relate the history of these reserves and the various discussions and negotiations that have taken place down through the years between the provincial government and the federal government would fill a good-sized volume. The first reserves were set aside when British Columbia was a colony, in pre-confederation days. Under the British North America Act, as hon. members are aware, the responsibility of looking- after the Indians is a federal responsibility. In British Columbia provision was made at the entry of that province into confederation for setting aside additional reserves as they became necessary. Various commissions of investigation were set up, one in 1875-76, to select reserves, but generally speaking the laws of British Columbia provided that the complete reversionary interest in the lands set aside for Indian reserves remained with the province. As a result of that, legal obstacles existed to the use of the reserves for the benefit of the Indians. For instance, if a portion of a reserve were surrendered it reverted to the province, and the province could sell it. If there were merchantable timber on the reserve, no disposition could be made of it without the proceeds going back to the province. That condition of affairs continued, generally speaking, until 1912, when both governments recognized that it was necessary to clear up the situation with regard to

Indian Reserves Mineral Resources
the resources on these reserves. Accordingly the McKenna-McBride commission was set up to determine the extent of the reserves and to consider matters generally affecting the Indians. That commission reported, and in 1919 an agreement was drawn up in accordance with the recommendations of the commission providing for the settlement of many of the outstanding difficulties. For some reason or another action was not taken on this agreement for many years, and it was not until 1938 that the lands were conveyed by the provincial government to the federal government.
To go back a little, a question arose as to the ownership of the minerals which might be found on lands transferred to the dominion in British Columbia, and a test case was taken to the privy council to decide the ownership of the precious metals. The privy council gave judgment that the precious metals belonged to the crown in the right of the province.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Has the minister the citation?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
The case was decided in 1889. An extract from the judgment of the privy council reads:
The precious metals in, upon and under crown lands, are not incidents of the land but belong to the crown, and, under section 109 of the British North America Act, 1867, beneficially to the province.
That judgment, of course, established that if precious metals were found on such lands, the dominion had no claim to any benefits arising from the exploitation of these precious metals.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: They belonged to the crown in the right of the dominion?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: No, the judgment was that they belonged to the crown in the right of the province, and consequently on Indian reserves they could not be utilized by federal authority for the benefit of the Indians.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I see.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
But that left the ownership of the base metals undecided. The government of British Columbia has not receded from the position that the base metals also belong to the crown in the right of the province, while the dominion government has held that they belong to the crown in the right of the dominion for the benefit of the Indians concerned.
During Premier Pattullo's tenure of office in British Columbia I had several discussions with him on this point with a view to having
it cleared up. The result of all the discussions which have taken place is really crystallized in the bill which we have before us.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Not in
the bill but in the agreement.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: In the agreement, yes; I accept the correction of the hon. member for York-Sunbury.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
May I ask on what
grounds you separate the base from the precious metals in a contention of this kind? Both are underground; would not both be subject to the same jurisdiction?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: The case before the privy council which I mentioned a moment ago covered only precious metals. As I stated, the province of British Columbia had refused to concede that it had not possession of the base metals as well.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I understand that.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: On the other hand that can be settled only through the courts, because the federal government held-I am not familiar with the precise legal reasoning in the matter-that the right to the base metals is with the crown in the right of the dominion for the benefit of the Indians. To cover this point an agreement was reached with the province of British Columbia relating to the manner in which the mineral resources on these Indian reserves might be developed. I am bound to say I think that in the agreement reached the British Columbia authorities have taken a fair position. Perhaps from their point of view it seems a generous agreement in this regard. At any rate the agreement has been reached.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Is it a fair agreement from our point of view?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
I shall deal with that in just a moment. If a difficulty arose, if it were determined that ownership of the base metals rested in the crown in the right of the dominion for the benefit of the Indians, we would have the dominion government for the Indians controlling the disposal of the base metals, and under the privy council judgment we would have the province of British Columbia controlling the disposal of the precious metals. Precious metals and base metals are frequently found in combination, and it does not require much imagination to see the problems and the difficulties which would arise under that condition. Consequently the agreement covers this. The provisions of the agreement which is being
