ratified under this legislation are that the prospecting and the development of minerals on the reserves shall be under the laws and regulations of the province of British Columbia; that is the province will issue permits to prospect, permits to develop, but only after the Indians concerned have given their agreement to it in the ordinary manner which is provided for in the Indian Act.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: That is the meaning of the reference here to getting the permission from the Indian agent? I understand that getting permission from the Indian agent means that the Indians themselves concur?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Yes, that is provided for in the Indian Act. The matter is placed before the Indians and they vote in the manner determined in the Indian Act as to the surrender of these minerals, and then the prospecting and development follow and are done under the laws and regulations of the province. There is a provision that the royalties or the revenues which are derived at present by the province under its laws from mining development cannot be reduced so far as these reserves are concerned without the consent of the federal government. In other words, those royalties and dues, if one may term them such, at present in force in British Columbia, are, I believe, as high as or higher than they are in most of the other provinces, and they cannot be reduced by the province as regards the minerals on these reserves without the consent of the federal government. The revenues derived from the exploitation of these minerals on reserves, whether they are derived from gold or from base metals, are divided equally between the provincial authority and the federal authority; the federal authority using them, of course, in trust for the Indians concerned.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: What use may the provincial authority make of the funds?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: They become part of the ordinary revenues of the province, and can, I suppose, be used in any way in which the province wishes to use them. What is sought in this bill, then, is confirmation of the agreement reached with the province of British Columbia covering the disposal and handling of these minerals on Indian reserves which may be found from time to time. I do not think there is anything I need add in explanation of the measure.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Is the share of the money which comes to the dominion held in trust for the particular tribe living on the reserve where the mine is situate?
[Mr. Crerar.l

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Yes, it is held in trust for the Indians on the particular reserve.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: The basis of the agreement arrived at between the dominion and the province results in an arrangement by which one-half of the revenue collected goes to the one and one-half to the other. Is that arrangement arrived at by an understanding that the values of the precious metals and the base metals are similar? The question arises in my mind, what to-day is a precious metal? Of course, gold and silver; but several other extremely valuable metals are now mined, a good many of them in British Columbia, which to-day may come under the category of precious metals. I should like the minister to explain on what basis the arrangement of fifty-fifty has been arrived at.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Well, ordinarily in the past such metals as gold and silver have been regarded as precious metals.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Platinum?'

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
I am unable to say whether or not platinum comes within the definition of precious metals. I am inclined to think that it does. In any case, whatever the regulations of the province may be in regard to royalties or the revenue secured from gold or silver or platinum or any other metal, base or precious, that scale of royalties and revenues cannot be reduced, as I have stated, without the consent of the dominion. Now, that maintains the existing scale of fees or royalties upon which the province derives revenue from the development of these minerals, that is over the province generally. In the second place there is no need, it appears to me, to draw any distinction between gold or minerals carrying gold and ores carrying, say, copper. I cannot at the moment say what the provincial government scale of royalties is, but assume for the sake of argument they have one scale of royalties for gold, another scale for copper, another scale for zinc. In any case these royalties apply whether the development on the reserye is gold, copper, zinc or all three, and consequently the interests of the Indians in that regard are fully protected. There is a definite advantage to the Indians of British Columbia in this arrangement, because it clears up any doubt that may exist as to the degree to which they might be able to participate in the development of minerals on the reserves. It establishes clearly and definitely what I think is a fair, if a somewhat rough and ready, rule for the benefit of the Indians. I will admit at once that if on these reserves base metals were found in large

Indian Reserves Mineral Resources
quantities and it could be established that the federal government had the right to the development of these for the benefit of the Indians, then possibly on balance the welfare of the Indians might suffer a little. On the other hand, if any future development were mainly in the precious metals, then the province would not do so well. As I have already stated to the committee, this is a rough and ready method of settling what has been a contentious subject and on a basis which, on the whole, I believe, will not detract anything in the end from the total revenues of the Indians by and large, having regard to what the situation would be if the matter were left in any uncertainty or doubt.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
The general principle of this bill is undoubtedly good because it does away with the objection that has been in existence for many years in British Columbia, that if the Indians-or anyone acting for them-discovered a valuable mine, it could never practically be worked because the other party, the provincial government or the dominion government, would step in and say, "You may take out your silver but you must not touch our lead, for instance." It ended practically in the Indians being deprived of any benefit whatever.
There are a couple of discrepancies, as I understand the bill. The explanatory note does not accord with the agreement. I was given to understand, in conversation with some of the officials, that the first procedure would be to obtain the consent of the particular band of Indians to surrender these minerals, and it was so stated in the explanatory note. The note has no legal effect whatever. It reads:
Briefly the arrangement provides that upon surrender by the Indians the administration, control and disposal of the minerals and the mineral claims shall be subject to the laws of the province.
That appears in the explanatory note which, as I say, has no legal force whatever. The real thing that does bind these people is to be found on page 3 of the bill:
The administration, control and disposal of all minerals and mineral claims, both precious and base, in, upon, or under all Indian reserves in the said province shall be subject to the laws of the province. . . .
"Shall be": in other words, the moment this bill is passed the Indian has no say at all in the matter. On the other hand the minister may point to the following provision which appears lower down on the same page:
And provided further that no prospecting or right of entry on the said Indian reserve shall be authorized or permitted until permission so
to do has been obtained from the Indian agent for such reserve; such permission shall be subject to such terms and conditions as the said Indian agent may specify and shall be granted only to such persons whose application for permission has been approved by the gold commissioner for the mining division of the province in which such reserve is situated.
That takes care of the white man and of the provincial government but not of the Indian. Elsewhere it states that on the passing of this act all these minerals shall come under the control of the province. I maintain that the procedure hinted at in the explanatory note, which, I repeat, has no force, should have been maintained, to surrender all the rights of the Indians in that particular reserve and, in the regular way, to have the Indian agent call a meeting of the band, whereupon he would ask if they would surrender the minerals on the reserve. Of course they know then what the deal is, and they would give their consent with a knowledge of the terms and so on. Anyone can come to prospect on the reserve-that is quite all right- but only with the consent of the Indian agent, and he may make such terms and conditions as he thinks fit. The act should be so worded as to provide that the protection afforded the Indian with regard to their consent will be safeguarded as in the Indian Act.
There is another objection I see, to which I would call the attention of the minister. I am sure it was not intended that we should arbitrarily take away the ownership of these minerals from the Indians without their consent. It is provided in the old act' that nothing may be alienated without the consent of the band being obtained, and that is as it should be; but in section 7 of this bill it is provided that the province shall run the whole thing, collect all royalties and so on, and give the dominion government one-half. That, too, is all right; but it enacts that the province shall not be liable to the dominion for failure to collect the revenue or any portion of it by reason of the neglect or failure of any officer or servant of the provincial government or of the department of mines of the province to carry out his duties in connection therewith. That is a very unfair provision. By force of law you will take the minerals from the Indians, admittedly a good thing, and make a deal with the province by which they will run the business and give the dominion one-half. But if they fail to do it, if some official neglects his duty, some servant of the province, the Indian is out of luck.
If you make a deal in a business way you are under obligation to carry it out; and it is not sufficient for me, if I enter into an

Indian Reserves Mineral Resources
agreement with someone and my servant does something that contravenes the agreement, to turn round and say: "I am not responsible; you had better see him." The deal is between the dominion and the province, and if the province agrees to collect the money, it should be responsible except where it is impossible to make the collection. It should not apply where there is wilful neglect on the part of an officer or servant of the provincial government. He might steal money, for instance, and the province might very well say that section 7 absolves it from liability. If the province fails to collect the money it should be liable. It is not sufficient for the province to say that one of its servants ran away with the -money. As I say, the provision should apply only where the failure to comply with this part of the agreement is unavoidable. If they made a deal with a mining company and the company went bankrupt and could not pay, then I would say it was not the business of the -province to pay what should have been collected; but where it is a matter of sheer negligence or malfeasance on the part of an officer, a man stealing money, for example, the dominion as trustee and careful guardian of the rights of the Indians should protect these people in such a way as to enable them to collect from the province whose servant was responsible.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
On the face of it there is some force on the point raised by my hon. friend. I do not see, however, where there could be any failure by which the Indians would suffer. It could not arise without the province suffering equally. If the servant of the province who has to do with the administration stole money he would be stealing the province's money as well as the Indians'. If he were negligent he would be negligent in his service to the province as well as to the Indians.
This agreement was the result of a rather rough and ready way of settling a contentious dispute. There is this to be said, that the province bears all the cost of administration and yet 50 per cent of the revenues derived are paid in for the account of the Indians.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Is it the gross revenue or the net revenue?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
It will be 50 per cent of the revenues received, according to the information supplied to me on that point. So that I do not think there is really any very serious obstacle to the ratification of this agreement in
IMr. Neil!.]
the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, though I recognize that there may be some force to it.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: What about the surrender?

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: On that point the agent will be governed by the instructions of his superiors. The Indian Act provides the basis upon which surrenders may be made, but as I recall it the act also provides in certain cases that if a band of Indians persists for some reason in pursuing a course that is really detrimental to their own interests, action may be taken to overcome that situation. I should say that in the actual administration of this matter the general terms and provisions of the Indian Act will govern, as they govern in other, similar matters.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Quite so; that would be the case if you had left the act as it was or if you had said that this procedure would be subject to the ordinary provisions of the act. But here you are devising something to take the place of the section of the Indian Act which now says you cannot take land away from a band of Indians without their consent, without calling a public meeting, and so on. There may be provision for dealing with extreme cases, in regard to the right of way for a railway, for example, but that is an extraordinary circumstance. The general principle laid down is that Indians may not be deprived of anything belonging to them without their consent, but now you are going to substitute the power of the Indian agent who can make conditions under which someone may go prospecting. I think it was intended originally that the right of the Indians should be surrendered in the usual way, and the explanatory note says so:
Briefly the arrangement provides that upon surrender by the Indians the administration, control and disposal of the minerals and the mineral claims shall be subject to the laws of the province. . . .
But that is only in the explanatory note, not in the bill. Nothing is said in regard to the surrender, however; it only states that the Indian agent may do certain things.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I think it may be assumed-

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Well, we cannot assume things.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Yes, I think it may be assumed that in the administration of this matter the provisions of the Indian Act will be observed. It is quite true that it does not say so specifically-

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Why not?

Indian Reserves Mineral Resources

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I do not know why, but that has been the practice in the past. The Indian Act provides for surrender being obtained from the Indians under certain conditions; but if a band of Indians, through some mistaken idea, follow a course that is against their own interest, I think I am right in saying that the administration has the right to overrule the Indians.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: That is only in an extreme case, and it is left to the judgment of the department, not to the whim of an Indian agent.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Oh, well; this will not be left to the whim of an Indian agent. An Indian agent would not act in a matter of this kind without consulting his superiors.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: As I see it, the question is not whether an Indian agent would or would not act. The question is, can he or can he not act; because if we give the Indian agent power, neither the government nor anyone else can say to him that he should not take this particular step. The fact is that we should so frame the legislation that there is no question of interpretation or assumption connected with it. The whole situation comes down to this, that if, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has pointed out, the Indian Act makes certain provisions, we should have something more than the minister's statement that he assumes the provisions of the Indian Act will be followed, or that he is quite sure nothing will be done contrary to its terms. It seems to me that good legislation, well drawn, would leave no room for doubt and would make it unnecessary for the minister to interpret the legislation, as he is attempting to do now. That is a job for the courts, not for the minister.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
I am not attempting to
interpret anything.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Well, the minister has mentioned certain assumptions, and so on. I think the point of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is well taken. If the terms of the Indian Act are to be read into the statute by those administering it, then they should be written into the statutes by those who are enacting it.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
I suggest an amendment, and a few words would do it. I would suggest that section 2 be amended, to begin with these words:
Upon the surrender of the minerals in any reserve, according to the terms of the Indian Act, the administration . . . shall pass to the province.
Then the surrender would have to be obtained in the usual way.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Of course this agreement has been confirmed already by the legislature of British Columbia.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
But we are legislating in
behalf of the Indians. We are their guardians; we are not worrying about what the province has done. We are putting through legislation that will affect the Indians, and I say they are not getting the full protection to which they are entitled. If you inserted the words I have suggested, they would be protected.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: As a matter of practical observation I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is tilting at a windmill.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Well, I was an Indian agent for ten years, and I know how the Indians look at these things.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I know also how the Indians look at these things. In actual practice what would happen to an Indian agent who, of his own volition, gave away rights in connection with these matters? He would not long be there. My hon. friend knows as well as anyone that the Indian agent must carry out his duties in conformity with the instructions issuecl to him.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
Absolutely; and in this case the procedure unquestionably will be that provided in the Indian Act for the disposition of assets on reserves. While it does not so state specifically in this agreement, I think to assume anything else is not in accordance with the practice of the Indian department or with common sense. It may be that my hon. friend is quite right when he says the agreement couldi have been drafted in clearer terms on that point. I am willing to concede that, but the province of British Columbia has passed legislation approving this agreement. It took a great deal of effort and persuasion to bring them to that point, and now if we should say, " We are not quite satisfied with this agreement and we want to amend it further," they might reply, "Well, we are through with it." I have no hesitation in saying that the settlement of these contentious points by this agree-

ment is m the interests of the Indians of British Columbia. I think my hon. friend will agree with that; there can be no question of it.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: I have said so already.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: That being so, I am prepared to recommend to the committee that we pass this confirming legislation now.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Of course the fact that the minister has brought in the bill indicates that he is recommending it to the committee, but I think he has to go a little further than that. I am interested in this. I know that the minister and the government, to put it in a more or less vulgar term, are rather on a spot in this matter, because of the fact that the agreement has already been signed. The bill itself is a matter of only two or three lines stating that the schedule to the act shall be confirmed and shall take effect according to its terms. I should like to ask the minister if, in the negotiations between the province of British Columbia and the dominion government, the question raised with respect to the provisions of the Indian Act applying in the event of surrender was discussed.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
No, not so far as my recollection goes. It was not mentioned at all, because how the Indians might give it up was not a question of concern to the province. What the province was interested in was the question of the disposition of a contentious matter, and the question of clearing up the matter of revenues, and the development of resources, should they be found. That was wrhat the province was mainly interested in. I have not the slightest doubt that if we had put into the agreement the most stringent possible terms to the effect that the vote of the Indians would be required, or a three-quarters vote would be required, or anything of that kind, the province would not have raised the slightest objection.
The point of criticism raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is that we are giving too much power to the agent on the reserve.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Too much power to the Indian agent.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext: Instead of to the Indians, to whom it belongs.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
But my answer to that is that, in effect, we are not giving power to the Indian agent. The Indian agent must carry out the instructions, regulations and

conditions of the Indian Act. I have not the slightest doubt that these surrenders will be secured in all cases from the Indians in accordance with the terms of the Indian Act, and in accordance with the practice that has obtained in connection with Indian administration all through the years.

subtopic: MEASUKE TO RATIFY AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING ORE DEPOSITS ON INDIAN RESERVES
speechtext:
If I were an Indian agent this is what I would look at:
,.^le. administration, control and disposal of all minerals and mineral claims, both precious
d base, m, upon or under all Indian reserves in the said province shall be subject to the laws ot the province.
_ Does the minister say that that conveys any instruction to me to go out and get the consent of the Indians? Not at all. The old Indian Act states that before any disposition of Indian lands shall take place, the Indians shall be called together, and that their consent shall be obtained. This deprives them of that opportunity, because it says the administration from this day on shall be subject to the laws of the province. What is the use of asking the Indians to release something that has already been taken away from them? The minister says he is sure that the Indian agent will do so-and-so. Well, if he knew Indian agents as well as I do he might not be so sure. Why bring legislation here if the form of the whole procedure is to be based on someone presuming that somebody else will do something else. The Indian agent does not have to do it, because the moment this bill becomes law and this parliament passes the legislation the administration and control will be subject to the laws of the province. Subsequently, in consideration of a capital sum of $3,000,000 which was made available for large scale improvements, largely in central Ottawa, the grant was reduced to $200,000 a year in 1928. I am not opposing the bill, because I am not anxious to be continually reducing expenditures. We get beauty by spending money, not by saving it. I am in favour of the bill, but I would make one suggestion. When parliament is ready to grant $200,000 a year for the purpose of beautifying Ottawa, I think the city should try to follow suit in some little things. It takes more than parks and driveways and canals and green grass and flowers and trees

to make a capital city. I hope I shall not be criticized too severely for what I say, but if you take the parks and trees away from Ottawa you will not have much left. The reply will be made that we cannot do anything without getting money from somewhere, but money is the hardest thing in the world to get under the present arrangement. If the Department of Public Works would spend a little more money upon our buildings it might be to the advantage of this city. There are some nice buildings in Ottawa, such as this one, but some of the dirtiest places in the city are those owned by the government. For instance, I never thought much of the Daly building. I do not know why they have the windows in that building painted green, but there may be some reason for it. For the most part the windows in our public buildings are very dirty, and that is not a good advertisement for government ownership. When some great operatic star comes to Ottawa, what happens? I do not think much needs to be said about this amendment. It is a desirable amendment and should have the unanimous support of the committee. When the bill was before the special committee in 1940 numerous requests were made that the maximum should be raised, some hon. members suggesting a limit of $3,000 or $4,000. My memory is that the committee was favourable to increasing the maximum, but the government was opposed because the schedules had been worked out and the

I never thought that that was correct because the inclusion of these higher paid employees under the act would have benefited from an actuarial point of view. As the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) mentions, the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act is to spread the hazards of unemployment over all workers, those who have fairly permanent employment and those who have only seasonal or part-time employment. If we were to eliminate from the act those who are in the higher wage brackets, then we are making a case for excluding from the act those who are in sheltered employment. If the insurance scheme is to apply only to those who are bound to be out of work for part of the year, it would not be possible to make the rates high enough to carry the insurance on an actuarial basis. I insist that all workers should come under the act, that there should be no exception or no ceiling as far as annual wages are concerned. In the meantime I think it would be wise to accept this amendment. If the department or the government feel that the maximum should be increased, I think it will meet the wishes of the labour movement in general. I am in favour of the amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, July 15, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Transport services-
1. Departmental administration, $26,960.
Does the minister propose on this item to make a statement with regard to wmr expenditures?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no elaborate statement to be made about war expenditures of the Department of Transport. These are really incidental expenses in connection with the ordinary services, but additional services are being provided. They are merely increases in some of the branches: for example, transport controller, merchant seamen, canals service, marine service, and railway and steamship service, and a special item for railway equipment; providing for loans to the Canadian National Railways for two purposes, namely increasing the equipment, and the development of the Vermilion oil field.
I believe these estimates would be disposed of more quickly if on each item the desired information was requested, and I would attempt to give it.

Item agreed to.
Director of merchant seamen-
Headquarters administration, $73,190.

Would the minister give the committee some account of the progress being made by the director of merchant seamen particularly with regard to the schools of seamen which have been set up, and how they are prospering?

As hon. members know, this service is required in order to furnish the supply of merchant seamen required for the boats which have to be manned from our several Canadian ports. Also the pool is operated to accommodate British as well as foreign seamen who arrive on our shores on either British or foreign ships. This is being done through a working arrangement with Britain, and the expenses of the upkeep and
War Appropriation-Transport

paj^ment of their basic wages while the seamen are here in the pool are reimbursed by Britain.
We have our pools in Halifax, Saint John, Montreal, and Vancouver, and we are establishing one at Sydney, a subsidiary pool to Halifax, in order to accommodate the merchant ships which come to that port. In each place we have what we think are, what we are trying to make, suitable quarters to take care of these seamen, who, when they arrive at our shores, never know, owing to the exigencies of war, when they will be called upon to go back. They cannot be expected to live on the ships, while they are waiting for the return trip. They receive their basic wage, and they are boarded and lodged in the pool until they receive employment. The great difficulty is to get trained officers in Canada. Heretofore we had a very small merchant navy. For the obvious reason that there was no great demand for officers, few of our boys trained. With the immediately increased demand we had to resort to Britain for our requirements, and I am happy to state that Britain has provided so far, and has given assurance that we shall be provided at least until September, sufficient officers to man the ships, and the crews will be Canadian. In view of the large requirements we have taken steps to provide for the training of some engineers and navigators. We have a school at Prescott, Ontario, and another school at St. Margaret's, Nova Scotia. Both schools have done exceedingly well and have provided quite a number of officers, who have been absorbed, as fast as they got their certificates, into our merchant navy. I may here give some details which might be of interest to the committee.
Each ship requires either forty-three or forty-seven officers and men. We get the officers from Britain and certified engineers and firemen from our schools. We expect that, if things go well, we shall have seventy-five ships manned by August-and not only manned, but sailing the high seas. We provide the ordinary seamen from Canada, and the officers, masters and other special officers, from Britain. The supply, as I have stated, has been practically guaranteed up to September next.
This is from the pools?
No, the officers are not taken from the pools.
No, not the officers, but the men.
All the men are taken from the pools.

When the minister moved into his estimates on the Department of Transport war appropriations, I was out for a moment when departmental administration, which is the item upon which I should really be speaking, was passed. I had previously spoken to the minister and told him that I had a remark or so to make with respect to the general transportation situation, and if I may be permitted to give it now, I should like to do so.
Much has been said in the house from time to time since the war commenced about the major contribution being made on many sectors of our civilian front. I desire briefly to speak of and to pay tribute to the yeoman service being rendered by these scores of thousands of our Canadian people engaged in the railway transportation services of Canada. In my young days I had the honour of being an employee of one of the Canadian railway systems. I know something of the esprit de corps and the tradition of the railway transportation services, and I felt that I could not let this opportunity pass without saying a word on behalf of a great and important section of our people who on the civilian front are rendering a magnificent service under most difficult and trying conditions.
We take these services, I fear, too much for granted, largely because they operate without seeking to draw the attention of the public in any comprehensive way to the work which they are quietly and constantly performing.
Outside of agriculture, railway transportation is perhaps Canada's biggest war industry, and has shouldered a burden of war activity the extent of which few people in this dominion seem to realize. In 1939, the year war was declared, our Canadian railways carried 17,000,000 passengers, while in 1942 the number had increased to 42,000,000. Strained as the facilities were to meet these constantly increasing demands, with a man-power situation which left much to be desired, the employees of our railways may take much pride in the fact that, out of the 42,000,000 passengers carried last year, only 380 lives were lost from one end of Canada to the other in railway accidents. If we bear in mind the swollen conditions of passenger traffic, and the added responsibility of moving special troop trains, the loss of life is amazingly small, constituting less than one person in every 100,000 persons carried. The efficient care and constant concern of the railwaymen for the safety of their passengers has been so maintained in these war years that the ratio of death through accident is actually much lower than it was in the leisurely years of peace.

War Appropriation-Transport
In 1939, our railways carried 69 million tons of revenue freight; in 1942, this was increased to 107 million tons.
What more could be asked of, and what more could be given by these loyal employees of both railroads? They deserve the undying gratitude of a thankful Canadian people who have seen them measure up on the civilian front in the same way as their brother-employees are doing on the sea, on the land, and in the air in our armed forces.
Among Canadian National employees who have joined up, there are in the navy sufficient to man nine destroyers; enlistments in the active army are sufficient to form six infantry battalions; and Canadian National men in the air force would establish eleven air squadrons. Add to this, 1,000 officers and men of the Canadian National Steamships on active service on all the seas.
As of November 30 last, which is the last record I could obtain, and perhaps these numbers must be increased because of lapse of time, Canadian Pacific Railway employees enrolled in the armed forces from the eastern and western lines, and from the overseas office included: 4,263, army; 1,039, navy; 1,622, air force and 686 others, making a grand total of 7,510. On active service from Canadian Pacific Steamships, express and air lines, there are another 6,087.
On the war front, and on the home front, Canadian men of the rails are giving their best, are giving their all, in the cause for which this nation fights so that it may be brought to a successful conclusion.
Hats off! to the railway employees of Canada. No tribute which this House of Commons or the people of Canada cam pay them will do justice to the contribution which they are so quietly but so effectively making at the present time.

I had hoped that the
minister, in describing what had been accomplished by the director of merchant seamen, would tell the committee something with regard to the school recently set up to which youngsters can go and be trained.

I was about to come to
that. I was going to describe the way we are trying to recruit crews for our Canadian-built ships. We have two training schools, one marine engineering instructional school, opened on January 1, 1942, at Kingston, but transferred on April 1 of that year to Prescott, Ontario, in a government-owned building. We have been training boys in marine engineering, the capacity being eighty trainees each six weeks, although the average has
been about sixty. I am glad to be able to say that these boys have all been absorbed and have given excellent service, and had it not been for these facilities we would not have been able to get the engineers required. The age limit is from eighteen to thirty.

What length is that
course of training?
' Mr. MICHAUD:	Six weeks. While they
are in that school they are lodged and fed. After they graduate from that school, if we have not immediate employment for them they are transferred to the manning pool waiting to be called for service. Besides this school at Prescott, we have one at St. Margaret bay, at Hubbards, Nova Scotia. It was opened in July, 1942. The capacity is 115 to 140 trainees over a thirteen-week period. The age for admission to the school is from seventeen to twenty-two. So far we have had an average of about 125 for each course, and these graduates have volunteered for service on completing their course. These are the two schools that are operated under the director of merchant seamen for the purpose of giving initial training to boys and men for the Canadian navy.
With regard to the second school the minister mentioned, does he mean that 125 are turned out every thirteen weeks?
Yes.

I wish to draw to the attention of the minister complaints that were forwarded to me by certain persons on behalf of the crew of the ss. Lady Laurier. The minister will recall that members of the crew of this ship some time ago staged a walk-out on account of the conditions prevailing on the ship.
I have a statement signed by two members of the crew which I should like to read to the committee. This indicates conditions which in my opinion are really disgraceful and which should not be tolerated if we are to have any hope of building up a merchant marine in this country. Though I did not go into the question of working conditions when we were dealing with questions of transport on the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply, I may tell the committee that practically the same conditions prevail on the Pacific coast. This statement reads:
To whom it may concern:
We, the following members of the crew of the ss. Lady Laurier, operated by the Department of Transport, do hereby swear the following to be true and correct.
After we had protested on several occasions against the wages and conditions on the above

War Appropriation-Transport
mentioned vessel, we gave fourteen days' notice of our intention of leaving the job, unless the said wages and conditions were improved. At the end of that time we signed off the articles, leaving the ship.
Having left the ship, several of us attempted to obtain employment on other ships through the selective service. We were told by the local agent of the selective service that we must either return to the Lady Laurier or go into the army.
Although only seven days' notice were required to leave a job and we had given fourteen days' notice, we were refused good discharges, were reported "DR" as to character.
I do not know what those two letters mean in seafaring parlance.
This discharge yvas issued without any shipping master being present, although the Canada Shipping Act states very clearly that it is an offence to give any such bad discharge unless entered in the official log of the ship and issued in the presence of a shipping master.
As I have already said, this statement is signed by two members of the crew. I should be glad if the minister would make a statement in regard to these charges.

I have never seen the declaration which has been read by the hon. member. If the members of the crew of S.S. Lady Laurier presented their case to their superior officers of the naval service of the Department of Transport, their grievance never came to my attention until a copy of a letter written by an officer of the Canadian Seamen's Union in Halifax to a member of this house was shown to me, in which letter this gentleman, acting in behalf of allegedly dissatisfied seamen, brought their case to the attention of the hon. member in question. When the matter was brought to my notice a few days ago I made some inquiry and found that on June 3 a certain number of the crew of the S.S. Lady Laurier informed the master that they would not proceed on the next trip unless they were granted a bonus of $44.50, which bonus should not be subject to the income tax. On the return of the Lady Laurier to port, these men were informed that their demand for an increased war bonus could not be met, and then on June 11 fifteen left the ship. They received discharge certificates marked "DR", which in the naval vernacular means " declined to report." The men were directed back to the ship by national selective service, a few days later, and apparently have resumed their work, and I have not heard from them except through the hon. member for Cape Breton South and this afternoon through the hon. member for Vancouver East. It is possible that these dissatisfied members of the crew of the Lady Laurier brought their grievance to the attention 
of the master, but the facts which I have related were brought to my notice only a few days ago.
The allegations set out in their sworn declaration are substantially what has been reported to me by the officer of the marine department. Their wages could not be increased on demand, because they are subject to the war labour board and also to the schedule of pay received by all seamen on government boats. I know that some of these ordinary seamen feel that they should receive higher wages, and in some respects I am inclined to agree with them. So much so that when this matter was brought to my attention I caused some action to be taken with a view to increasing some of their allowances as much as was permissible within the rules. If this cannot be done to the extent I feel it should be done, then the matter will be brought to the attention of the war labour board and a request will be made for the increase which I believe they should be given.

I will just give the minister and the committee a few figures with respect to wages paid on the ss. Lady Laurier. A fireman receives $80 a month. Added to that is board amounting to $19.50. In the month of June, the month in which the dispute on the Lady Laurier took place, the men had worked twenty-seven days on the ship. All in all, able seamen on the ship averaged fifteen hours a day. That is, for the twenty-seven days in June they worked 374 hours. Since this item has to do with merchant seamen, I presume I am in order to speak on it, although I did not know that the Minister of Transport had anything to do with this subject. It appears that on December 19, 1942, order in council P.C. 11397 was passed. Perhaps I might invite the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) to this, because it seems to be under

his jurisdiction. Apparently there had been an order passed some eighteen months before that, known as the merchant seamen's order. The purpose of it was to expedite the departure of ships, but apparently it was not working very well for it was amended five times. Then, in December last they wiped out the whole thing and started afresh. My opinion is that they have not made things much better.
The order works something like this. The Minister of Justice may nominate two men, and two men only, to compose a committee of investigation which may inquire into the conduct of any seaman, picked up when and where you like. This investigation is preliminary to an inquiry which may be held later on. One man represents the naval services and the other the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but it really means that one man is the committee, because subsection 3 of section 3 of the order states that the naval service man shall be the chairman and his decision shall prevail. In other words, he is the whole committee. As I say, this committee has authority to investigate the conduct of any seaman wherever he may be.
The evidence may be taken by way of affidavit. Any lawyer will know how unfair that type of proceeding is to the accused, because the man who is giving the evidence by affidavit cannot be cross-examined, and there is no chance to have him modify the affidavit which he may have made weeks or months before. The case might arise when some captain or mate is busy loading a ship and is anxious to get away. A seaman comes along, perhaps after having a drink or two, and gives the officer some impudence. Next day the officer goes and makes an affidavit, but the case does not come up for a week or a month. By this time the officer may be at sea, and the affidavit cannot be modified as perhaps he would like to do. As I have said, there is no opportunity to cross-examine. It will also be remembered by those of us who are familiar with the naval and marine services that there is a vast difference in discipline between the two. Is it not Shakespeare who says:
That in the captain's but a choleric word,
Which in the soldier is flat blasphemy.
In any of these shipping towns you can hear language among seamen which would be very different from what would be allowed in the naval service. Their relationships are much more easy in the merchant service.
This investigation is to determine whether a prima facie case has been made out against the man, but nine times out of ten the man

War Appropriation-Transport
is not there and knows nothing about it, and the investigation is held in his absence. This investigation is held on the strength of the affidavit of a man who made it weeks or months before and has probably gone away and forgotten all about it, or, if he thinks about it, wishes he had not made it.
I particularly call attention to the circumstances under which the committee can order a man arrested. He is not summonsed; he is arrested and put in gaol. Under the various subsections of section 6 of the order this one-man committee can issue an order to arrest a seaman if this one-man committee is satisfied-that is the criterion-that he is "likely to be" responsible for causing any delay in the departure of a ship or is "likely to refuse" to sail on a ship or is "likely to refuse" to perform his duties on a ship or is "likely to induce" other seamen to interfere or is "likely to carry on" any subversive activities. The committee does not have to be satisfied that the man has done any of these things-not for one minute. It has only to be satisfied in -the man's absence that he is "likely" to do them. I suppose the committee looks at a man's photograph and says: "This is a bad man; we do not like his looks; we will send him to gaol because he is 'likely' to do anything." We are all "likely" to do anything, and if all of us here had to go to gaol because of things we are "likely" to do, it would be just too bad.
A sailor can be arrested without warning simply because this one-man board thinks he "is likely to" do something. Is it anything approximating British justice to arrest a man because somebody thinks he "is likely to" do something wrong?
Having ordered the man's arrest, the committee finds a prima facie case against him and submits it to the board of inquiry. The board of inquiry is appointed in the same way -no; it is even worse because the procedure there is this. The board of inquiry supposedly consists of a representative from each of three different departments, but it is provided that two will suffice and that where a quorum consists of two only, the decision of the chairman shall prevail. Another one-man court, and it all boils dowm to an officer in the naval service.
It is also provided that the original committee, or one member of it, shall be a competent witness before the board of inquiry. There is another case of making the thing a hole-in-the-corner affair. There again the board is empowered to convict this man just because he is likely to do something or to refuse to do something. How in the name of providence can you know what a man is likely to do until
you tell him to do it? You take a look at him, I suppose, and say: "He is bad medicine; we will put him in gaol for three months." They can give him three months in gaol, but before the end of the three months he is brought forward again, and after taking into account the seaman's "attitude"-they take a look at him, I suppose, and say, "we do not like his looks"-if he comes up smiling, he is impudent, and if he looks gloomy, he is sullen -in any case he is a bad egg-after taking into account his attitude, if they think his attitude is not exactly what they like, they can send him back to gaol for six months. It is three months the first time, then six months, and if a total of nine months is not enough they can recommend his internment. They can at any time adjourn, and in the meantime the seaman has to stay in gaol. There is no sworn information laid as we know it in ordinary cases. There is no trial by a magistrate. The trial takes place before this self-appointed board of inquiry where the seaman has no advocate and no choice at all. He is not tried before an ordinary magistrate. Does not magna charts preserve the right of everybody to be tried before a jury of his peers? Can you call a naval officer a suitable man to be the peer of a seaman in the merchant service? I am not a lawyer, but I can see that there is no protection there for the seaman.
I would ask, is this procedure fair; is it just, or is it justified? Because some drunken sailor, perhaps meeting the mate off his ship in a saloon, using sailor language says to him that he will be so-and-so if he sails under such a slave driver, he can be railroaded into gaol for nine months and interned thereafter.
I am not exaggerating at all, because the committee:
. . . may in any case wherein an investigation has been conducted, direct in writing that any seaman be temporarily detained, if it is satisfied that there are grounds for believing that such seaman-
Remember it has only to be satisfied that there are grounds for believing; it has not to be convinced at all.
(a)	has been responsible or is likely to be responsible for causing delay in the departure of a ship.
A telegraph boy carrying a telegram may delay the sailing of a ship. Is he to go to gaol or be interned? Then (b):
(b)	has deserted or is absent without leave in Canada from his ship.
That is reasonable. Then (c):
(c)	has refused or is likely to refuse to sail on a ship;
(d)	has refused or is likely to refuse to perform his regular duties on board a ship;

War Appropriation-Transport
(e)	has induced or attempted to induce, or is likely to induce or attempt to induce other seamen to interfere in any way with the proper operation of the ship.
If one man says to another, "Thi3 is a h

of a hole," that, I suppose, is attempting to induce another seaman to interfere with the operation of the ship. Then (f):
(f)	has carried on or is likely to carry on any subversive activities, whether on board his ship or otherwise.
And then the same process is repeated all over again. We are supposed to be fighting a war for liberty. I remember that some years ago the then Minister of Mines and Resources, at the instigation of an Indian agent., brought in a bill making it a criminal offence liable to six or twelve months in gaol for a man even to think of holding a potlatch, which is an illegal ceremony, banned by the government, quite properly, in connection with certain Indian rites. That was to give the Indian agent some help in securing a conviction, because before that you had actually to catch the Indians doing it. So that he got the government to bring in this clause which said that a man could be hauled up and punished if he only had it in his mind, and the person who decided whether it was in his mind or not was the Indian agent who had him arrested. If you call that British justice! It only had to be presented to this house to be laughed out of court; it was so utterly against every principle of justice. Suppose there has been some trouble with a ship getting away; then by all means punish people who do anything subversive in the way of holding up a ship or trying to induce other men not to work; but why should a seaman be subject to all these restrictions and injustices? Are we to go back 200 years, and restore the methods of the press-gang, when they went along and dragged away a likely-looking man and put him in the hold and he found himself 200 miles at sea a day or two later. They used to do those things, but we do not do them now. Why should we inflict such a severe penalty without anything being proved against a man except that he may be likely or he is likely to do so-and-so? I do not expect the Minister of Transport to answer; possibly he knows nothing about it; but I should like the Minister of Justice to give us his idea as to whether he thinks that is justified.
I did not catch the first few sentences that the hon. member stated. Would he be kind enough to give me the number and the first few words of the order in council of which he is complaining?
Yes.

At the Government House at Ottawa Saturday, the 19th day of December, 1942. Present: His Excellency the Governor General in Council:
Whereas by order in council P.C. 2385, dated 4th April, 1941, an Order Affecting Discipline of Merchant Seamen was made, to 'be cited as "The Merchant Seamen Order"-[DOT]
That is under the authority of the governor general.
And whereas the purpose of the said order is to prevent delay in the departure of merchant ships from Canadian ports during the present emergency, and to provide that if delay occurs or is anticipated as being likely to occur by reason of the activities of a member or members of the crew of any such ship, there can be taken in respect of such member or members of any such crew such action as will prevent delay in the departure of any ship, and which will serve as a deterrent to members of the crew of any other such ship who might contemplate like activity.

I think that explains the reason for the order in council. That is a war measure, passed to prevent mutiny, delays in sailings or departures from ports, through some members of the crew who might be on board as spies, or unfriendly, thereby developing a situation, which would hold up the whole crew and the boat. These rules are made to assure the disciplining of that person or those persons, and at the same time prevent during war time the delaying of merchant ships which might have to depart at a certain moment and, indeed, must depart at the moment which is stated, on account of the difficulties of sailing on the high seas through enemy interference. The order is made for that purpose. It is a war order.

The minister used the word
"mutiny." Lord bless me; we have never been in sight of mutiny. It says, if you are "likely to do" these things, "likely to refuse" to sail-
Well?

Not, that the man has refused
to sail-
That is mutiny.

-but that he "is likely to."
Has anything happened in the last few years in connection with sailing ships which would justify such an extreme measure? I recall an occasion when a Turkish sultan boasted to the English ambassador, "I know how to stop crime. There was a baker discovered giving short-weight in his shop one day, and we put the baker in his oven and baked him, and there has not been any case of short-weight

War Appropriation-Transport
since then." But that was a long time ago, and that is not the British system of doing things.

My hon. friend understands that during the war all kinds of nationalities are represented in the crews of these ships. When foreign ships or British ships arrive at the port of Vancouver or Halifax or Saint John we do not know the character and background of these men. This was passed to prevent any possibility of any one or two or more men on board a ship holding up the ship for a few days and preventing its sailing when the road is clear.

The minister says that we
do not know the background of these men, and their character, and what they are likely to do. I do not know the background of half the hon. gentlemen in this house and I do not know what they are likely to do.
You have a pretty good idea in some cases.

We do not know what we
would do under temptation. Some of us are likely to do anything.
My hon. friend does not suggest that we apply these rules to the members of this house.

Absolutely. If it is good
for one man it is good for another. You cannot show that there is any mutiny or delay on ships, and you are taking an enormous power which cannot be justified. I will sit down and say no more if the minister says that it is a square deal. I ask him if he thinks it is.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Has the hon. member any factual case to which have been applied any regulations which would violate the rights of a man concerned? It sometimes happens that these war orders are drawn by gentlemen who have recently come into the service and who make them just as stringent as the English language can provide. I have been concerned about the terms of some of these orders. I have had a number of them redrafted, and have expressed to those who are charged with enforcing them that mere convenience was not enough to justify departure from the ordinary rules of procedure, that it is only when it is necessary for the security of the state that there should be any such departure, and many of them have been "toned
down," shall I say, in expression. If the hon. member knows of any case to which rules have been applied which have really prejudiced the man's rights and the manner in which he should be treated, I should be glad to know the facts and I would at once follow the matter up-*

You might tone it down a bit.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: -and point out how this power should be used. I have had to make, at the request of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, quite a large number of appointments to committees of this kind, and no instance has been called to my attention of harsh or unfair treatment having been meted out to anyone. But even that, I would admit, would not justify some of the terms which apparently are included in this order. I do not remember when it originated, but had it been one of the orders submitted to the department recently for redrafting it would not be in that form; and had there been any case in which a man's rights have been interfered with it would have come to my attention.

Not necessarily. The statement made by the Minister of Justice is entirely satisfactory to me. If he makes the statement that he will look into that particular order in council I shall be quite satisfied with what he does with it. I have not any specific case before me. I am not familiar with what goes on around Montreal, or even Vancouver, but the very fact that the order is in effect indicates that it will be used from time to time. If the minister will look at it and agree, if in his judgment it is necessary, that it be redrafted, I would be perfectly satisfied.

Since the order has been passed, no case has been brought to the attention of the Department of Transport where any seaman has had occasion to complain, or where it has been necessary to apply these rules.

But take a man from Yugoslavia, or Russia, or Liverpool as far as that goes, and he gets a raw deal in Montreal or Vancouver; can the minister tell me what facilities an ignorant man has for reaching him?
I think they can find channels, and they do complain.
