It belonged to the West Indies line. It was torpedoed, and it was thought by both the underwriters and the officials of the company that it would be cheaper to refloat and refit the boat and put her back into service than to build a new boat to take her place.
Who owns the ship now?

The crown will own the boat, and I suppose will have to fight it out with the Canadian National as to whether the salvage would have been greater than the amount spent to refit her. But that matter has not been determined yet, because the boat is not in commission.
Was she insured?
Yes.

I think this would be an appropriate place for me to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport the disaster which took place in Bedford basin a short time ago, in which nineteen lives were

lost. I realize, of course, that a public inquiry is in progress at the present time. I am most interested in providing equipment in the future, such as diving equipment, so that it may be on hand to be used immediately for rescue work, in the event of our being so unfortunate as to meet again with such a disaster. I am informed there is no suitable equipment at Halifax or at Bedford basin, and I believe there should be. I have received letters asking me to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, and I do so knowing that he will realize the importance of Halifax harbour, and the dangers which must lurk there on account of the heavy traffic passing in and out. I would ask him to take these points into consideration, having in mind the possibility of procuring diving and other equipment which might be required.
This question is now under consideration.

Item agreed to.
Purchase of railway equipment for Canadian National Railways, 1941 orders, $4,883,664; 1942 orders, $24,543,000.

We have very little opportunity to discuss either in the committee or the house matters affecting the Canadian National Railways. Therefore I shall take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the committee a condition existing in respect of trains operating out of Halifax. I recently made an inquiry of the minister, in reply to which a return was tabled a few days ago. My question had to do with the number of trains operating between Halifax and Moncton and Moncton and Campbellton. The reply I received was that whereas there were three trains operating between Halifax and Moncton, there were four operating between Moncton and Campbellton.
This is not a question of my province against the minister's native province; it is not a question of Nova Scotia against New Brunswick. But the minister cannot help being aware of the heavy traffic being carried at the extreme eastern end of the Canadian National Railways. He knows that practically no train leaves Halifax which is not overcrowded; and that applies to all trains. The Ocean Limited and the Scotian leave in the morning, and the Maritime in the afternoon; and all are crowded. I would urge that the minister take into consideration the providing of extra trains to fill the much needed requirements from Halifax northward.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in giving details as to population, the number of stops and the places served by these trains, but I would say that the three

War Appropriation-Transport
trains running between Halifax and Moncton serve a population of 127,000 along the line, as compared with a population of 43,000 or 44.000 served by the trains running between Moncton and Campbellton.
Then, I would bring to the minister's attention the matter of the running time, particularly as it applies to the Maritime. The running time of that train is eight hours and thirty minutes from Campbellton to Halifax. It appears to me, and also to a great many rail-waymen who have been in the service for a long time, that this train could be speeded up to a certain extent. This would help to relieve the situation, and give the minister an opportunity to provide additional trains between the others I mentioned, namely, the Ocean Limited, the Scotian and the Maritime. It might be possible to put on additional trains, or to add second or third sections to the trains now running.
We in the maritimes certainly appreciate the good service we receive from the Canadian National Railways, so far as they are able to serve us. This observation applies particularly, I believe, to train crews and the handling of freight. But I must say we are not satisfied with the passenger service, because we do not think the community is being served in the manner in which we believe it should be served.

I can appreciate what has prompted the senior hon. member for Halifax to present his case. I know that on many previous occasions he has described the situation to me, and of course he is more familiar with local conditions than I am. Nevertheless he must realize the situation which exists on the railway lines between Moncton and Halifax. If there is any shortage of passenger facilities between those points, he will understand it is not owing to any ill-will, negligence or antipathy on the part of railway officials. It is owing to conditions which are well known, and cannot be overlooked. However, I shall be pleased to direct the attention of the administrators of the line to the remarks of the hon. member.

May I thank the minister
for his reply. However, I would emphasize one point I made in only a casual way. There are four regular trains serving the district between. Moncton and Campbellton, whereas there are only three between Halifax and Moncton. In view of the respective populations of these communities, I say that service should be reversed, and there should be four trains between Halifax and Moncton and three between Moncton and Campbellton. I leave that point with the minister.

I agree that in normal
times what the hon. member has said might be so. But he must realize that there is a tremendous congestion of traffic between Moncton and Halifax, a much greater amount than on other sections. Three lines meet at Moncton. There is a single track from Moncton to Halifax.

Is this amount for
rolling stock and equipment?
Yes.

Is it for passenger and
freight engines and oars? May I say, incidentally, that I believe the Canadian National Railways are giving a splendid service. We have to use the railways a great deal in travelling from here to the west, and I can state that both railways are doing their best. However, there is a terrific shortage of equipment, and perhaps we have had a good opportunity to note that fact. The senior hon. member for Halifax has probably noted the shortage in respect of dining-cars. I have seen people standing two or three hours in line to get into the car for their meals. I believe that is due not only to the shortage of dining-cars, but also to the shortage of help. How is this sum divided? Are freight cars receiving priority, or does the priority go to passenger cars or to engines? What is being done?

I am afraid the hon.
member will be disappointed. There is no provision for passenger accommodation. We have to give priority to other equipment, and in these days it is impossible to get passenger equipment out of the shops. I shall give a list of the requirements covered by these amounts.
Out of the 1941 appropriation of $25,000,000 there is a balance of $4,863,664.23 unexpended. This is to cover the cost of 742 box cars and fifty baggage cars. On the 1942 programme there is an amount of $24,543,000 to cover the cost of thirty locomotives, 300 refrigerator cars, 1,750 hopper cars, 200 flat ears and 4,000 box cars.

I realize that under war conditions freight cars should have a priority, *but the fact is that there have been lay-offs in some of the railway shops. I do not know very much about the Canadian National shops, but I do know there have been lay-offs in the Ogden shops at Calgary and I believe there have also been some at the Transcona shops. I wonder if we have not reached the point where, if we can get steel, we should be able

War Appropriation-Transport
to utilize some of these men who are experienced in building railway cars to build more passenger cars, even if we have to make a larger appropriation. As I said before, the railroads are giving the best service they can under very difficult conditions, but the travelling public is feeling the effect of the shortage of railway accommodation.
I fully appreciate what my hon. friend has said, but he has touched the point when he says, " if we can get steel." If we could get steel, we would do it.

Item agreed to.
8. Loan to Canadian National Railways for development of Vermilion oil fields, $600,000.
Could the minister give us some particulars of the work that is being carried on in the Vermilion oil field and the progress that is being made?

This is a loan to be made to Canadian National Railways. On October 1, 1942, an order in council was passed authorizing the incorporation of a company to be operated by or on behalf of Canadian National Railways to carry on the development of the Vermilion oil field. The Canadian National Railways investigated this oil field and alternate sources of supply and recommended the development of this field of over 600 acres, which is sufficient to support fifty productive wells. Another order in council was passed authorizing an advance by way of loan to Canadian National Railways of a sum not exceeding $1,000,000, with interest at three and a half per cent per annum, repayable in five years. The subsidiary company is to refund to the railway company the net proceeds from the sale of oil after proper royalties, interest, operating and other incorporate expenses have been paid, the railway company in turn to apply such proceeds to the reduction of such loan. Any remaining obligation to the government when the operations are wound up are to be discharged by Canadian National Railways.
Is the Canadian National Railways actually drilling wells and producing oil?
That is what I am informed.
For its own use?
I do not know to what extent.
Surely it would not be producing oil to sell in competition with other producers?
Not to compete against oil producers.
Why was it necessary for the Canadian National to go in there? Was the company which is in there already not producing sufficient oil?

This matter was discussed on a former occasion by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The actual working would not come under our supervision; we have it incidentally because the sum was advanced through the Department of Transport to Canadian National Railways.
Do I understand the minister to say that drilling is actually being done by the railway company?
No, I am not saying that. I know they have commenced to explore or to get something under way, but I do not know to what extent.

I understand that a
separate company was incorporated to carry on this work?
That is true, authorized by the order in council.
And this money is being advanced to that company?
The subsidiary company, through the Canadian National Railways.
What is the name of the company?
Cannar Oils Limited.

Do I understand that $600,000 has been given to Canadian National Railways, directly or indirectly, to gamble on the development of oil in this field, and a further $1,000,000 at three and a half per cent to permit the development of oil? Have any results been shown so far? This seems to me to be an extraordinary step, one in which a major policy is involved.

As I said before, the Minister of Munitions and Supply who is responsible for this project has already given an explanation. I understand that the dominion geologist, the oil controller and officials of Canadian National Railways were satisfied that the purpose for which this oil might be required would justify an investment of $1,000,000, and the Canadian government has agreed to lend the money to the Canadian National Railways at the rate of three and a half per cent per annum, to be repayable in five years. Canadian National

War Appropriation-Transport
Railways are authorized to advance money to the subsidiary company, Cannar Oils Limited.

What particular facilities have Canadian National Railways for the development of oil? If the Minister of Munitions and Supply is the instigator of this expenditure of public moneys, why does he not set up a company which would be able to retain professional oil people who might know something about the business? I know of no one on the staff of the Canadian National who could qualify as an expert in oil drilling. This is an extremely hazardous business. A great deal of money has been sunk in attempting to bring in wells in western fields, sometimes with success but naturally more often without success. I think the committee is entitled to know what reasons there were for advancing $600,000 in one case, and $1,000,000 additional by way of a loan with the expectation that some oil might result.
It may be true that dominion geologists say there is a prospect of developing oil in a certain field, but geologists have often said that a structure is such that there might be oil there and nothing results. Everyone knows there is perhaps no greater gamble than attempting to extract oil from the bowels of nature. I think the committee is entitled to a full explanation of the reasonableness of this appropriation and the method by which it is proposed the money shall be spent, namely, by the Canadian National instead of by a separate government-owned company, or perhaps by private enterprise. The house argued for some time when the budget resolutions were being considered in an endeavour to make it more feasible or more possible for private enterprise to develop oil with some expectation of profit where wells were discovered in western fields, but without much success. The Department of Finance did not hold out much prospect of the venturesome capital which might be successful in producing oil retaining fairly adequate profits. Yet we find the government putting in its own money through an organ of the government, namely, the Canadian National, which to my mind is fitted in no way whatsoever for the development of oil in this country.

That may be so, but the Canadian National is a great consumer of fuel oil, especially in western Canada, and is equipped with a department of national resources of its own to investigate sources of supply for its requirements.
Someone has asked if this is to compete with private producers. This is a development of the Canadian National Railways to 72537-313
provide its own oil requirements for its operations in the west. Those who come from the west know that in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan the railway needs large quantities of fuel oil for its operation, and this is an investment made to assure, if possible, a supply of oil for the requirements of the railway. It is being undertaken by the railway itself just as it looks after its other requirements, and we consider that the railway should take the responsibility of undertaking this development. I understand that the Canadian National have taken the precaution of consulting government geologists and the scientists of their own staff, and I have no doubt they have retained the best brains possible to help bring this field into production in order to assure a sufficient supply of oil for their requirements in the west. The fuel oil supply in the west is a difficult problem, and it may become more difficult. The Canadian National Railways have had to import large quantities of oil, and if the source of supply were cut off, it would be very unfortunate.

I do not think the Canadian National Railways are taking any chances, because the Vermilion field is already proven; anyone passing on the train can see dozens of derricks all through that district. It is a good proposition.
And they are producing the oil.
Yes, and there is a refinery there, too.

I think the railway is to be commended for undertaking this work and developing that field. I am very glad to see it, and if the railway can provide fuel for its engines, so much the better for itself and so much the better for the country. I hope it will strike oil richly.

The hon. member who spoke a moment ago should not confuse the Wainwright-Vermilion field with the Turner valley field in regard to the cost of drilling. The wells in the whole Vermilion area are shallow, and the cost of drilling a well there is negligible as compared with the cost of drilling in the foothills area farther to the west. As the minister has just said, the oil produced in the Vermilion area is a very low-grade crude oil and cannot be treated in the same way that the finer oil nearer to the mountains is treated and refined into gasoline.
I do not think the Vermilion oil is refined before it is used in the railway's locomotives.



War Appropriation-Transport
It should also be borne in mind1 that practically all the locomotives on the main line of the Canadian National Railways are oilburning.
I believe that the depth of the wells in the Vermilion area is under 2,000 feet, so that it is not as expensive to drill there as some people may imagine.
I have been trying to make the estimates for transport services under the war appropriation measure as set out on March 3 in Hansard tally with the items which are on this sheet before us.

Air services are not
included in the main estimates.

Take, for instance, item 3 on this sheet: Director of Merchant Seamen. The amount on the sheet is a little over one million dollars, while the item given in Hansard on March 3 is just under one million dollars. Again, with regard to item 6, additional harbour facilities at Halifax, the amount on the sheet is $481,000, and the amount in Hansard of March 3, $281,000. What explanation is there for the items not agreeing?
New requirements.
Is there an increase here over what the Minister of Finance put before us in Hansard?
I do not think so.
They do not agree anyway.
Item agreed to.

Mines and geology branch-
Investigations of petroliferous deposits and of potential petroliferous areas in Canada, $500,000.

Last night we asked the minister what exploratory work was being done for oil deposits, and the minister in reply covered pretty exhaustively the work that is being done on the prairies and in the north. I was wondering what was being done on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and in other parts of Canada in the way of exploration for new fields.
The minister said last night that $42,000 had been spent on an investigation of the shale deposits of New Brunswick?
What about the Gaspe peninsula?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
None of this expenditure is for the Gaspe peninsula.
Before I answer my hon. friend's question I want to correct an impression that was given last evening when we were on these estimates and I was speaking of the number of parties that would be financed out of this vote. We have made provision in the ordinary estimates for a number of parties; they will be paid for out of the ordinary estimates, but additional parties may be sent out and paid for out of this vote. I think I mentioned last night that seventeen parties would be taken care of out of this vote, but that is scarcely an accurate statement. I am not able to say just how many parties will be taken care of out of this vote, but I shall have more information when the main estimates are before us later.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I find there are a number of parties here, but generally speaking the search for oil is being carried on in Alberta and northeastern British Columbia. I mentioned last evening one party which was working, I think, in southwestern Saskatchewan. In addition, there was an expenditure in New Brunswick on the oil shales, and also some expenditure in Nova Scotia, but not of a very large amount.

Item agreed to.
Mines and geology branch-
To provide for special exploration and development work in connection with the supply of strategic minerals, $500,000.
Where is any development work going on-not exploration, but development?
This is for special explorations and development work in connection with the supply of strategic minerals.
I understand that. What I want to know is, where is any actual development going on, under this vote?

It was approved on the recommendation of the metals controller and the director of the mines and geology branch. Before any of the money is spent, the metals controller has to make a recommendation and it has to be concurred in by the director of the mines and geology branch. When these two officials agree, the matter is submitted and certain projects or explorations are undertaken and are cared for out of this vote.

Was there an item
under the same heading last year?

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources

Yes; last year there was
released from the war appropriation $413,500, and I think $323,520 was spent. I do not know whether all the $500,000 will be used this year or not. It is simply an estimate of what may be required. It may be that not more than half will be spent.
How much was exploration and how much development last year?

Pretty nearly all was
development work, loans to companies, to be repayable out of their earnings, in the search for strategic minerals. There were administration costs, which last year ran to over $13,000. Then there was an equipment pool; that was a pool of diamond drills, drilling machinery, and the like, which could be used and directed from one point to another point. Many of the concerns did not have equipment of that kind and could not get it, so that this pool was provided. Let me repeat that all this was done on the recommendation of the metals controller.
Then, fluorspar was a mineral in considerable demand and of considerable importance, and arrangements were made with several companies for the development of fluorspar deposits which they had, but which they were unable to proceed with unaided. Money was advanced under agreements recommended by the metals controller, the advances to be repaid out of the proceeds of the fluorspar produced.
Chromite was another one. An arrangement was made with the Base Metals Mining corporation to carry on certain exploratory and testing and drilling work on certain zinc deposits in one of the western parks.

That was not a Base
Metals mine; that was another mine?
That is correct, I am advised. Then, $5,000 was provided to the British Columbia war metals research board to carry on certain work.

That was returnable
too?

No; that is not to be
returned. That was really for scientific investigation work by this board.
What 'board is that?
It is the British Columbia war metals research board.

Is that under the provincial
government bureau of mines?

It is connected, I understand, with the university of British Columbia.
Then we have scheelite, from which tungsten is derived. That is very important. Some of the gold mines have scheelite in association with gold. That is particularly true of the northwestern part of Quebec. Therefore the scheelite concentrator at Val d'Or in northern Quebec was assisted to the extent of $7,000.
The manganese deposit in Nova Scotia was assisted to the extent of slightly over $19,000. There was another tungsten deposit in Nova Scotia, upon which almost $29,000 was spent. There is another item, Orford Mining company ; I think that was for chromite. Chromite Limited received $82,000. Another manganese concern received a very small amount, $927. Then there was a molybdenite deposit in northern Quebec.
Where was it?

At Quyon, Quebec, not
very far up the river. I understand it received assistance to the extent of almost $7,000. Then there was a molybdenite deposit in British Columbia which was examined, on which $4,000 was spent. An examination of the possibilities of tin was made at a place called Rush lake, in Manitoba. There are tin deposits there, and examination was made as to the quality or grade of the deposit.
Was any money advanced in connection with the discoveries of manganese in the vicinity of the Manitoba lakes?

No. I am just running
over the various projects, in reply to the request of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
Would the minister give in each case the name of the company and the amount received?

The Rush lake investigation was carried on, I am informed, by officials of the department. I do not know who owned it. Then there was the Regal Snowflake concern in British Columbia. That involved $3,200. Then there was the H. C. Miller fluorspar deposit in eastern Ontario, $26,000, and another fluorspar deposit, Trent, Fluorspar company, in which $3,700 was spent. That generally describes the nature of the expenditure. In some cases this would be recovered; in other cases, if the deposit is not a commercial proposition it will not be. The need for all these so-called strategic metals has been very pressing, and in no case was the work undertaken except on the recommendation of the
4954	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
metals controller, whose recommendation was concurred in by the director of the mines and geology branch. There were a good many proposals put up that were not considered worthy of investigation. That is briefly the type of thing that has been going on.

Does this department or the national research council do any work in connection with the finding of aluminum clays in Canada? If so, with what success? Some work has been done in the Dakotas south of Saskatchewan and stretching towards Manitoba. There are clays, I know, in the Dakotas, of the type we have in some parts of the prairies, which contain not as much aluminum as bauxite, but a considerable amount. If supplies were difficult to get, or if the submarine menace increased, which I do not suppose it will now, that might be a strategic mineral. Has the department done anything in experimenting with these clays, or have we any such clays in Canada? I am told that such clays exist immediately south of the prairies, in the states to the south.
So far as Canada is concerned I have no knowledge, nor has the department any knowledge, of any bauxite.
Not bauxite.
Well, no, not bauxite, but any clays of a kind that will produce the raw material for aluminum.	,

I believe that some
slight investigation has been made by the university of Saskatchewan and they have discovered some very low-grade aluminum clays. I believe I am right in that.

Of course, no specific search has been made. Perhaps that is not the correct way of putting it, but there has been an alertness to learn of any deposits anywhere that could be utilized in the production of aluminum. Certainly, however, it has not been brought to my attention, if there are such, and I know that no recommendations have come from the metals controller for the development of such deposits. That does not say that they may not exist in Canada, nor does it say that somewhere in Canada at some time we may not find bauxite. I think it unlikely; but as hon. members know, there have been developments in the last year or so, which were discussed by the Minister of Munitions and Supply when his estimates were up, out of which has developed the production of magnesium metal. I understand that there is a considerable quantity of raw material, ores or clays, out of which magnesium metal can be made in Canada, and it may well be that such metal in the future will be a

competitor with the aluminum metal. I understand that magnesium metal has the qualities of aluminum and the virtue of being lighter.

Of the amount expended last year, how much went to private companies? I understand that under the regulations any work that is undertaken other than by the Department of Mines and Resources must be under agreement or contract approved by the governor in council. How much was actually expended by grant to private corporations? How much has been expended in Saskatchewan in connection with this work, and has not the department of natural resources of the province brought to the attention of the minister certain possible areas where strategic metals can be found? If so, where are those areas?

I have not the detailed information to answer the first part of my hon. friend's question, as to how much was spent through the agency of private companies. I read the names and gave the assistance they received. These advances to companies are all made by order in council on my recommendation, but that recommendation is not made to council until a request is received, supported by the metals controller.
Are they all repayable?

Some are repayable. For instance, we may make an advance to some company and the judgment in regard to it may prove to have been wrong. There is a certain element of risk, but wherever a company gets into an operating position and can repay, it is expected to repay, and the agreement calls for repayment with interest.
In regard to the other question raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, I doubt if there has been anything in the nature of an active search for strategic metals in Saskatchewan. I think it is a fair assumption that the northern part of Saskatchewan, and particularly the northeastern part of the province, which is in the so-called pre-Cambrian shield, will undoubtedly in time develop mines. There is on the border of Saskatchewan and Manitoba the mine of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting company at Flin Flon. But these expenditures for strategic minerals were directed to the places where it was thought most likely they could be found. That again was done on the judgment of the officers of the department, who are supposed to know. None of these investigations was carried out simply for the pleasure of spending some money. They all had behind them some reasonable prospect of

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
being valuable in supplying these metals, some of which were in very short supply and were greatly needed in the war effort.

Did the department of mines of Saskatchewan not bring to the attention of the minister or his department certain strategic metals which it believed could be found in certain parts of northern Saskatchewan, at the same time designating where those metals were believed to be available?

I cannot recall at the
moment, but I think I am correct in saying that all the provinces have been bringing to the attention of the department here the possibilities in their respective provinces. I dare say there were hundreds of these prospects placed before us, a great many of which were not acted upon. The investigations that were actually made, or the engagements that were entered upon, were on the recommendation of the metals controller, as I said a moment ago, supported by the director of the mines and geology branch.

Apparently there were no investigations carried on in Saskatchewan, since, if I understood the minister aright, no expenditures were made in that province. There is widespread complaint in Saskatchewan because it seems impossible to get any cooperation from the metals controller for consideration being given to northern Saskatchewan. An outstanding friend of the government in northern Saskatchewan-I am not going to mention his name unless the minister asks for it-has brought to the attention of the metals controller certain metals that he believes exist there in such abundance as to be of assistance to the war effort of this country, but he has been unable to get any consideration whatsoever. I feel that if the provincial department of mines brings these matters to the attention of the government, its recommendations should be acted upon. We in Saskatchewan have a large area in the pre-Cambrian shield. There is now an opportunity under this vote to determine whether or not these areas contain metals which are needed at the present time. The provincial department of mines and resources has devoted its energies over a period of years to ascertaining these localities; yet that province has not been given any assistance under a similar vote last year, and we have been afforded no opportunity whatever to assist in the war effort in this regard.
I ask the minister during the coming year to see to it that we receive at least some consideration in this connection. As far as the war effort is concerned, little industry has been
established in Saskatchewan and little consideration has been given the needs in this regard of that province. I quite realize that there should be some probability of success before an area is examined and prospected under this vote. Many areas in northern Saskatchewan have been carefully examined by the provincial department of mines, and I ask the minister to see to it that this year some of this money is spent in that province, to the end that we may be enabled to contribute our share of the mineral needs. Apparently no money has been advanced and no assistance has been given to mining development in Saskatchewan, and no official in Ottawa can determine, without some investigation, whether or not strategic materials are available there.

Of course I shall give heed to the plea advanced by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I do not know that he would suggest that the department should go over the head or back of the recommendations of the metals controller, or act in these matters without those recommendations. I am not exaggerating when I say that scores of these prospective mines have been brought to the attention of the department. Naturally people who have mines of this kind, who think they have fluorspar or scheelite or molybdenite, believe there is a possibility of getting some public funds to assist in the development of their properties, and my hon. friend has had sufficient public experience to know that one must be very careful in, shall I say, resisting some of the requests that come in that way. I have confidence in the metals controller; he is a man of great experience in the mining business, and I think is a mining engineer by profession, and I have every confidence in the technical officers of the mines and geology branch of the Department of Mines and Resources.

And have they
recommended against Saskatchewan?

'No; they have not recommended against Saskatchewan, but I would say that no proposals have come to my attention concerning Saskatchewan which have been recommended by the metals controller and the director of the mines and geology branch. It is not a matter of recommending against something; it is a matter of recommending in favour of, recommending positively instead of negatively. I may have erred, and the government may have erred, but we felt the safe course was to follow the advice of the people who we thought were qualified to give advice in these matters. This does not mean that the provincial department of mines and
4956	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
natural resources has not been active. As I said a moment ago, I think all provincial governments have brought to the attention of the department here the possibilities that existed in their provinces, and have asked that something be done to explore those possibilities. Rightly or wrongly, however, we have adopted the rule that we would recommend to council only those proposals which, in the judgment of the experienced men who were advising us, were entitled to consideration.
May I ask the minister if there are not large deposits of dolomite in northern Saskatchewan?
There may be; I cannot say.

I have been told there are; and if there are large deposits of dolomite, perhaps the government should take the same action to assist in the production of magnesium metal in Saskatchewan that they took in regard to the production of magnesium metal in the Ottawa valley. In Saskatchewan the government would have to find power, just as the Ontario hydro electric commission found power for the magnesium plant at Haley station. I am firmly convinced that there must be a distribution of industry throughout Canada, and if there are large deposits of dolomite in northern Saskatchewan, power can be developed. I know where a substantial block of power can be developed, and if you put the two together you get magnesium metal.

I do not have quite the confidence in some of the controllers that the minister has. I believe that when this exploratory work is being undertaken, the northern part of the province of Saskatchewan does offer a field for exploration for a good many of these things, as the hon. member for Lake Centre has said. When the minister pins his faith entirely upon the metals controller, I do not think he is wise. I remember that a year or two ago the matter of iron ore on the Pacific coast came up; but in spite of the forceful presentation made by hon. members from the coast, and in spite of the fact that to me the evidence they presented was fairly conclusive, the only reply they could get was, "Well, you have not a ghost of a chance," merely because there was an established industry in another part of Canada. That is, virtually, the point of view. I think I would put much more faith in the report of the minister's own geological branch, as a matter of fact. They are public servants, who cannot look at it from the point of view of established industry.

But' I think we need to diffuse industry across the country. It is perfectly true, as the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, that in Saskatchewan, with all our resources, we have been unable to get any development during the war, for war purposes, which would assist us after the war in solving some of our problems in that area. We have potential power on our rivers, much more, I believe, than is generally supposed. And we certainly have an extremely large potential power supply in our very large deposits of comparatively low-grade coal, a kind of coal which has been used in Russia and in Germany for the production of power. And probably with the resources we have developed, industries could be established in some of these areas. I saw one hon. member shake his head' when I spoke about the low grade of coal utilized in Germany for power purposes. They utilize brown coal, which has even fewer British thermal units than the gray coal which we use in the southern part of our province.
I know that the Alberta coal is much superior. But in our gray coal we still have a source of power. I was not speaking from guess-work, when I spoke a few moments ago about the possibility of finding not bauxite, but clays which do contain a fair, and perhaps a commercial percentage of aluminum. I was surprised that the minister knew nothing about it, because I know some work has been carried on in connection with testing some of these clays.
By private parties?
By the university. I am surprised the minister did not know anything about it, and I would suggest that some inquiries be made.

Does the hon. member know where they are making alumina from
clays?

No; but I can say this, that we do know that there is more than one process of making aluminum. The process being used at the present time is the established process, because all the equipment made and used by the company which has the monopoly of that business is of the one type. But it is known' that there are other processes which might utilize the lower grade clays. How economical that would be, I cannot say.
I agree. I was interested in the hon. member's statement. I believe it is well known that all clay contains more or less alumina.

Some.

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources

Some clays are much richer than others. There is a gentleman right here in Ottawa, I believe, who for a number of years has been doing research work throughout the continent. But I have yet to find any instance where a process of extracting alumina from the aluminum clays has been demonstrated to be economically feasible.
That is, of course, an important point for consideration.

I have two questions to ask the minister, the first of which has to do with the long list of metals which he enumerated. In view of the expenditure of money, my first question is this: Is the minister in a position to tell us if help has been given to companies for development work, and if some of these moneys have been expended in that way? If so, have those expenditures been the means of producing certain quantities of the metals he enumerated?
My second question has to do with exploratory work in connection with iron ore. It is a well-known fact that the iron ores in the lake Superior area may not last longer than another ten years. I am speaking of the openpit method. It may be that we shall require all the iron ore we can get in Canada, and I am wondering if in the exploratory work the minister is seeing to it that the deposits or iron ore in Canada are being tabulated as to quantity, location and iron content. To my mind it is extremely important to do that sort of thing. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, we in British Columbia have been endeavouring for many years to develop a steel industry in that province. Time and again w'e have been met with contradictory reports-reports from private mining companies, provincial reports and federal reports, all conflicting. In view of the seriousness of the iron ore situation, and the extent to which iron ores may be required in this country, I say it is incumbent upon the government to see to it that exploratory work is done. Under this or any other grant, what has been done with regard to iron ore? Then, of the various metals enumerated, have any quantities been produced?

In some instances substantial quantities of these strategic metals have been made available as a result of this work. I do not know the exact amount of tungsten, for instance, that has been produced in Canada in the last year; and I do not believe it would be wise for me to give that information if I did know. Generally speaking, however, it may be said that
this expenditure has justified itself for the purpose for which it was initiated, namely to aid in the war effort. Probably if there had been no war, nothing of this kind would have been done in Canada at the present time, because we would have been getting our tungsten, molybdenite and chromite from other sources.
With regard to the hon. member's second question, there has been, of course, the general geological survey work, such as has been carried on in Canada for many years. This work has been done not only by the federal government but by many of the provincial governments, as well. All those geological reports are available. Iron ores of a very good grade indeed-I might say of a high grade, and in considerable quantities- are available about 130 miles west of Port Arthur. This is an ore similar in quality to that produced in the Duluth area. The total amount, however, is not yet known. It would require some years of exploration to ascertain that fact. A few years ago the development of a large body of low grade iron ore was undertaken in the Michipicoten area. A considerable amount of the iron and steel used at the "Soo" comes from that development. It may well be that there are other deposits of iron ore in Canada.
Here I would add that, certainly as a post-war work, this country should do a great deal more than it has done in the past-in my judgment, at any rate-by way of carrying out geological surveys and geological mapping. It has not always been easy to get the appropriations which those acquainted with the possibilities of this country thought were necessary. But I do say that I have great confidence in the future of mining developments in Canada. We may reasonably expect to find mineral-bearing rock all the way through this great preCambrian shield from Labrador, skirting northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan right through to the Arctic ocean. There are mines scattered all over that area and certainly, when the war is over, this development will be a means, not only of adding to the national wealth and providing employment but also to furnish all the benefits that come from such a development. Undoubtedly the possibilities are very great. One of the things needed for development is that as accurate knowledge as possible be secured from geological surveys and mapping.

There is just one suggestion I should like to make. This appropriation of $500,000 is wholly inadequate. More money should be spent on exploration for and development of strategic minerals. This
4958	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
vote only goes to show how difficult it is to find and develop a mine. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand the procedure is that a prospector comes to the department with evidence of a certain deposit, shall we say of scheelite, cinnabar or one of the strategic base ores necessary for the development of required metals. The department will then decide to send an engineer or surveyor to inspect the deposit based upon geological maps or whatever is known already of the district. If the department decides to *go ahead and considers the deposit worthy of exploration, is it developed by the department, or does the department assist the prospector to develop it? How does the prospector develop it?
If an established mine, say in the Porcupine camp, finds, as many of them have there and in northwestern Quebec, that there is a deposit of scheelite in their property which is not normally workable, does the department agree to assist that mine in the development of the scheelite? Does it tell the mine to develop the scheelite, the department paying for the out-of-pocket expenses? Does the taxation department say that it will reimburse the mine for the expenditures or allow them to consider it as development work which would be deducted from their taxation? This development work is one of the most important things that can be carried out, both now and post-war.
Before the war we knew nothing about what we could do in the way of magnesium, in the way of the development of iron ore, the development of mercury or of many other metals. These metals are being developed to-day, although it is true that some are being developed on an uneconomical basis. We who are in the business believe that the production of these strategic metals will continue, that they will be a part of the Canadian economy from now on. That is why I say this sum of $500,000 is inadequate.
I do not think the committee realizes just how little we are doing in the way of geological surveys as compared with other countries.
I do not want to belittle the geological survey of Canada, because the work being done by Doctor Camsell is simply magnificent, but it is quite small when compared with what is done in other countries. Either the year immediately before the war or the year before that, the United Kingdom actually spent more on geological surveys than did Canada. We think of England as being a small country which has been prospected over quite a bit, but this fact shows the importance of the geological survey. When the story is finally 
written I think it will be shown how difficult it is to discover a mine. Considerable money has been spent on many prospects, but I do not know how many actual properties have been brought into production. I gathered from the minister's statement that it is not much more than one in a hundred.
I do not think we appreciate how difficult it is and the amount of money that must be expended in finding a mine and bringing it into production. This shows how wrong and how stupid it would be for the government to go into the mining business and develop mines as government property. The government should do everything it can to assist individuals in developing mines, so that every ton possible of useful ore is produced, but in my opinion the government has no business to go into the actual mining of metals and ores. As I say, this $500,000 is in my opinion a very small amount to be expended on the discovery and development of strategic metals during this war crisis. I should like to see the amount increased, but I hope the minister will state that it is not the policy of the government to go into the mining business and develop these things as government properties, except perhaps under extremely exceptional circumstances.

I think it is well to keep in mind that the expenditure under this vote is necessitated by the needs of war. This expenditure does not, except perhaps indirectly, have a bearing on what might be described as the general development of mining in Canada. The united nations and Canada were short of certain strategic materials, and we sought to see what could be done in Canada to supplement these needs. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, I have entire confidence in the integrity of the metals controller.
I am not questioning his integrity.
I do not think the metals controller has been doing chores for any person in connection with the work he has carried on. I think it is only fair to say that.
I was not referring to that.

I quite understand that. The hon. member for York West inquired if assistance would be given to a prospector who might bring in a prospect. If, upon inquiry, it were found to have merit, we might decide to carry on diamond drilling, as has been done in other cases, but the prospector would not be reimbursed for any expenses which he might

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
have incurred up to the time he had brought the matter to the attention of the government. In a few cases further exploratory work has been undertaken by the government in order not to pass over any possibility of adding to the store of these necessary metals.
As to the general question of the basis of mining development in the future, it will be the aim of the government to carry on the necessary services, geological and mapping, by the best men we can get, so that we may get as complete information as possible on the geology of the country, and then make that available to prospectors and developers and let them do the rest of the work. That at any rate is the basis upon which our mining development has been done in the past, and though it may change in the future, I am expressing my own view of what is the wisest course to pursue.

I can see no justification whatever for the expenditure of this money in utilizing the services of conscientious objectors. These men are paid fifty cents a day and remain in these various camps at work for a period, generally speaking, not exceeding three months. At a time when there is a shortage of man-power which has been so frequently referred to, in connection with the production of firewood, pulpwood, and for farm labour, I think there is no justification for the utilization of the services of these men in the national parks, particularly when this vote is considered as a war expenditure. Conscientious objectors should be permitted to serve in some service other than active war participation; as to that there can be no argument. But as far as the work being done in the national parks is concerned, it is a use of man-power for purposes unconnected with the war effort, and, I submit is an unjustifiable waste of man-power when regard is had to the needs and requirements of manpower in more necessary kinds of work. I cannot understand the justification for increasing the expenditure this year by approximately $250,000. Only recently in Saskatoon some seventy-five Doukhobors came before the national selective service board. They were allowed to work on their own farms; yet, with the imperative need of mobilization of our man-power, many of these people serve in connection with work in national parks. Their services could be used in agriculture. According to the statistics given in "Canadian Affairs", to which I referred the other evening, there are 3,401 in this country. An amount of $500,000 seems like a terrific expenditure to make for a matter of a few months' alternative service in parks. I move that this amount be reduced to one dollar.

I should like to say a word endorsing what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said and at the same time

to ask some questions in regard to the item. I cannot see any reason for this amount being expended at the present time. Last night we listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as he pointed out that we had 30,000,000 bushels of grain standing in cars on the tracks which could not be loaded into terminal elevators because we were short of man-power at this particular time. We have had radio broadcasts and what-not with regard to the shortage of fuel for next year, and municipal officials pointed out to the government, last fall and in the winter, that wood camps should be set up for the purpose of providing fuel for the coming winter. There is certainly plenty of all-year-round work to do now which would be of greater advantage to the nation as a whole than this proposed expenditure of public money. It is essential work that is required if the people are not to freeze this winter. In the fall we shall have to store grain, which is vital for feed, because the transport system is tied up as a result of the falling down of the selective service in that respect. I suggest that we should not waste this amount of money with the man-power muddle right on our doorstep at the present time.
I believe the government received communications last fall, in December and since then, from provincial and municipal organizations, pointing out that lands should no,t be sold to conscientious objectors at this time, but that they should be held until after the war for our veterans. So far I have not heard any answer from the government in that regard, and this might be a proper item under which to ask the minister what the stand of the government is in this respect. In his province and my native province the department of mines have intimated that they will not sell land to anyone until the war is over, so that the returned soldier shall have the first option on any lands they hold. We should have a statement from the minister as to the policy of the government in this matter. In all seriousness I suggest that we should consider eliminating this item, because it is a waste of public money and involves a waste of man-power which is so essential in other callings at the present time, in the national interest, if we are to obviate a great deal of suffering in the coming year.

The hon. member for Lake Centre spoke, I believe, without that reflection which he usually gives to his observations. He based his criticism wholly on expenditures that had been incurred prior to fifteen months ago, indeed, incurred over two years ago. The figures he read from the auditor general's

The situation two years ago in respect of man-power was vastly different from what it is to-day. My hon. friend knows that, as does every other hon. member in the house; and the problem when these men were called up was to find employment for them. At that time the national parks constituted one place where they could be employed and they rendered excellent service. They did very good work in the national parks. The situation has now changed altogether. I have stated in regard to other votes that they were estimates, and so is this vote an estimate of what might be required for this purpose in the present fiscal year. At May 31, there were 190 conscientious objectors working in the national parks, and on June 12 there were seventy-six in forest experimental stations. What were they doing? They were employed largely in Alberta to cut pit-props which are necessary in coal mining in that province. That is work which everyone will agree has to be done, because if you are to mine coal you must have pit-props. These men were engaged also in some parks cutting lumber and cordwood. So that if my hon. friend persists in the motion, which would have to be voted down, we would interfere at once with the production of necessary pit-props for the mining of coal, and we would cut down substantially the quantity of cordwood that is now being cut by these conscientious objectors and which is necessary to meet the fuel shortage next winter. I would ask my hon. friend, on reflection, to withdraw the amendment to the motion.
What I have said is, I believe, a partial answer to the hon. member for Souris. There is one point, however, with which I wish to deal that touches on his remarks. I refer to his statements regarding the sale of lands to conscientious objectors in the various provinces. The sale of land comes wholly within the jurisdiction of the provinces. It

may be that under the War Measures Act-it would be stretching it to a very great degree, as I think hon. members will agree-it might be possible to take some action federally, but it would be a pure invasion in a matter which it is solely the right of the provinces to deal with, and I think it would be resented by the provinces.
Not entirely, if the federal government owned land.
We are not selling any federal lands. If my hon. friend will give me one instance-
That is what I am asking.
There have not been any such sales. Why does not my hon. friend ask if there are instances?
The policy is what I want to know.
He rises and makes a statement that can only be regarded as a criticism of the government because we have not done something in this matter.
I did not make any such statement; I asked the direct question. What was the policy of the government?

Very well, then; I will say this, that as far as the federal government's policy is concerned, it has no lands to dispose of excepting certain crown lands, and I am sure none are being sold to conscientious objectors. I think those are all the lands it has, unless we go away up into the north-west territories, where conscientious objectors do not wish to settle.

There are other lands which I cannot discuss under this item, but which come under the same minister. I refer to soldier settler lands, and there surely would be a policy covering all the lands owned by the federal government.
I do not think any soldier settlement lands have been sold to conscientious objectors.

I am asking the
question.

goes, not a single foot of any land under the control of the federal government has been sold or disposed of to conscientious objectors; I am sure I am correct in that statement.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; the hon. member is putting an entirely erroneous construction on what I have said. The general principle is that property and civil rights are within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, but in war time it is felt by the Department of Justice that under property and civil rights the provinces must not be allowed to nullify war measures adopted by the federal authorities.

I quite agree, but the matters we are discussing now are in relation to the war. We are not talking about after the war; the matter we have raised at the present time is in connection with the war, and the minister's statement was in relation to the war.

speechtext:
Shall the amendment
carry?
Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those in favour will kindly say, aye.
Aye.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those opposed will kindly say, no.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In my opinion the amendment is lost.
Mr. Chairman, it was eleven o'clock before you put the vote.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall I report progress?
Progress reported.
It being three minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Saturday, July 17, 1943
